the Argives are proclaiming a sacrifice for the third day from now, and that all maidens are to go to Hera's temple; X, perhaps γ; nothing depends on it

borrow from me thick-woven clothes to wear, and gold; X, perhaps F offered; nothing is taken and nothing follows
strangers ... are rising from ambush towards the household. Let us escape the villains by flight; X; Orestes stops her

He found what he could, cast out of the house; dishonour of the corpse; nothing later depends on it

go to my father's dear old servant ... bid him come ... and provide something for the guests' meal; X; brings the old man

his father, the horseman, was training the son of Thetis as a light for Hellas; X

I have come, bringing you from my own sheep this newborn nursling of the flock ... and garlands, and cheeses; X; brings the old man to the recognition

stand in the footprint and see if the tread of the boot will measure with your own foot / "How could there be an imprint of feet on a stony plot"; X, perhaps Q−

tell me, what should I do to avenge myself on my father's murderer and on my mother; the hero asks for help; his want of vengeance was stated in ev 16, so X
all that you have is in your own arm and fortune ... "Kill Thyestes' son and your mother"; the answer to the hero's request, help given (counsel), so F; perhaps B

I shall prepare my mother's slaughter!; Electra undertakes to act against the misfortune

O Zeus, god of my fathers, be also the vanquisher of my enemies ... "Give us victory"; X
if you fall dead in the struggle, I am also dead ... for I will strike my heart with a two-edged sword; an intention, X; only her abortive move of ev 66 follows

he persuaded Atreus' own wife to secret love, and carried off to his house the portent; seduction and theft; nothing in the play depends on it, so no move

Zeus changed the radiant paths of the stars, and the light of the sun; X, perhaps U
I hear a wailing that means bloodshed ... "Mistress, Electra, leave the house!"; X

I report to all his friends that Orestes has conquered, and Aegisthus, the murderer of Agamemnon, lies on the ground; X; the announcement of ev 80
I could not recognize your face out of fear; but now I know you well; X
when he saw us, he called out, Welcome, strangers! Who are you and from where do you come?; the hero arrives unrecognized; answered by recognition in ev 83
We are Thessalians, going to the Alpheus river to sacrifice to Olympian Zeus; false words to get hold of the victim

Just now we purified ourselves in clean water ... we are ready and will not refuse; X

may my enemies suffer—meaning you and Orestes; a curse not carried out, X
my master prayed for the opposite, not speaking the words aloud, that he might win his father's house; X
take the knife, stranger, and show us if the report about the Thessalians is true; the hero is tested; perhaps θ, since the victim puts a knife in his killer's hand

the portal vein and near-by gall-bladder revealed threatening approaches ... "I fear some treachery from abroad. Agamemnon's son is the man I hate most"; X
let someone bring me a Thessalian axe and let me split the breast-bone ... "He took the axe and cut"; the hero gets the weapon; perhaps X
As he was bending down, your brother rose on tiptoe and struck him on the spine; his back-bone broke apart; the villain is killed; the messenger calls it that "Orestes has conquered"
the servants ... rushed to arms, many to fight against two; yet Pylades and Orestes in their bravery stood to face them; X, perhaps H or Pr; no blow is struck

They, when they heard his words, held back their spears; the want is met by the answer itself, so K; perhaps Rs
he was recognized by an old man, who had been long in the household. Immediately they crowned your brother with a wreath; the hero is recognized, answering his arrival as a stranger
Set your step to the dance, my dear; X
O glorious victor, Orestes ... receive this band for the locks of your hair; X, perhaps W (honour)
I am bringing you his corpse, which, if you wish, you may expose as prey for wild animals; X, perhaps U
whoever ruins another's wife, in secret love ... "you made a shameful marriage with my mother"; past seduction; nothing later in the play depends on it
[Spurning the corpse with her foot] Begone, knowing nothing of how you were discovered and paid the penalty in time; X, perhaps U
you must carry the body of this man inside and hide it, slaves, so that when my mother comes, she may not see his corpse before her slaughter; X; keeps the trap hidden
finely she walks to the middle of the net. —And here she comes, splendid in her chariot and dress; X
How can I kill her when she bore me and brought me up?; X, perhaps δ; draws Electra's urging
You who declared I was to kill my mother, whom it is clearly wrong to kill; the hero is ordered by the oracle to act
Do not become a coward and fall into unmanliness! ... "The same death that you gave to her husband, Aegisthus"; the want stated before, X, perhaps B
I will go in; it is a dreadful task I am beginning and I will do dreadful things; the hero agrees to act
Come out of the wagon, Trojan maids, and take my hand, that I may step down from the chariot; X
These slaves are here; take no trouble on my account; X
Tyndareus gave me to your father; X, perhaps W
that man went from the house, taking my child, with the persuasion of a marriage with Achilles, to Aulis; deceit to get hold of the victim; nothing later in the play depends on it
there he stretched Iphigenia over the pyre, and cut her white cheek; a killing; given as Clytemnestra's cause for ev 4, which is told earlier, but nothing later in the play depends on it, so no move
because Helen was lustful and the one who had her as a wife did not know how to punish the betrayer; betrayal; no move
he came back to me with a girl, raving and possessed, and put her in his bed; a wrong to Clytemnestra; nothing later depends on it; perhaps X
as soon as your husband had started from home, were adorning the golden locks of your hair at the mirror; X
you did not assign to us our father's home, but you brought the goods belonging to another to bed, buying your marriage; the children dispossessed; nothing later depends on it
your son Orestes and I must kill you to avenge our father; a threat, X
I will forgive you; for I do not rejoice so very much at what I have done; X
why do you not recall that exile / "l am afraid; I am looking to my interests, not his"; X, perhaps F−
You have heard, I suppose, that I have given birth; in thanks for this, please sacrifice; false words to get hold of the victim
But I will go to make the tenth-day sacrifice to the gods for the child ... "Take this team away, my attendants"; the victim is taken in and sends away her guard
Go into a poor house ... "the knife sharpened, the same that killed the bull by whose side you will lie, struck down"; X; she enters the house where she is killed
O children, by the gods, do not kill your mother; a plea, the asker's want first stated, so a; refused, nothing depends on it, so no move
O God! Ah me! ... "overpowered by your children"; the killing of the villain, told as "retribution for my father"; perhaps I; Electra shares the act
here they come from the house, defiled in the newly shed blood of their mother ... [The two corpses are shown.]; X
how the unhappy one threw off her robe and showed her bosom in the slaughter; X
she clung to my cheeks, so that the sword fell from my hand; X
I threw my cloak over my eyes, and began the sacrifice by plunging the sword into my mother's throat; the same act as ev 111, told again, so X; it fulfils the Chorus's prophecy
I urged you on and put my hand to the sword together with you; X; part of the act of ev 111
I am putting this cloak over the one loved and not loved; X
Having just now calmed the swell of the sea ... we have come to Argos when we saw the slaying; X
Give Electra to Pylades as his wife to take to his home; an order; carried out in ev 134; perhaps K (undoing ev 10)
but you leave Argos; for it is not for you, who killed your mother, to set foot in this city; an order; perhaps A (driving out) or U
the dread goddesses of death ... will drive you up and down, a maddened wanderer. Go to Athens and embrace the holy image of Pallas; a prophecy, fulfilled in the pursuit of ev 135
savage Ares killed Halirrothius ... in anger for the unholy violation of his daughter; X, perhaps A or U
An equal number of votes cast will save you from dying by the verdict; for Loxias will take the blame; a prophecy not fulfilled within the play, X, perhaps Rs
the dread goddesses ... will sink into a cleft of the earth beside this hill; X
You must found an Arcadian city beside the streams of Alpheus; an order; nothing in the play follows from it
the citizens of Argos will cover it in the earth in burial; X
Menelaus, who has arrived at Nauplia only now after capturing Troy ... "she has come from Proteus' house, leaving Egypt"; X

Menelaus ... will bury her, with Helen helping him; X
let Pylades ... go home from the Achaean land, and let him conduct the one called your brother-in-law to the land of Phocis, and give him a weight of riches; an order; Electra's departure follows
once you have completed your appointed lot of murder, you will be happy; X
Throw your arms in close embrace about me; X

Go, Pylades, and be happy; marry Electra; the marriage bestowed, carrying out ev 119; the wedding itself is not shown
go towards Athens, seeking to escape these hounds of hell, for they are pursuing you fearfully; the hero is pursued, as foretold; closes the play
who went to fetch the golden fleece for Pelias; Jason sets out on the Argo; departure assigned to its performer though he is not the play's hero; X also possible
my own mistress Medea never have sailed to the turrets of Iolcos, her soul with love for Jason smitten; Medea leaves her home; β considered

beguiled the daughters of Pelias to slay their father; harm by deception and killing; η/θ considered for the beguiling, taken as one act (A: "deceives to ruin"); Pelias' house remains her foe (S134) and she cannot return (S064)
come to live here in the land of Corinth with her husband and children; settling in Corinth sets up the marriage; nearest ↑
Jason hath betrayed his own children and my mistress dear for the love of a royal bride, for he hath wedded the daughter of Creon; abandonment and remarriage, the harm the play turns on

Creon, the ruler of this land, is bent on driving these children and their mother from the boundaries of Corinth; a rumour of an intended act, carried out at ev 15; nearest A (intended, not done) or B
Do thou keep them as far away as may be, and bring them not near their mother in her evil hour; an order; nothing later turns on it
Curse you and your father too, ye children damned, sons of a doomed mother! Ruin seize the whole family!; a curse, treated like a prophecy fulfilled by the children's death; no function
O, to see him and his bride some day brought to utter destruction; a prayer to Themis and Zeus, first statement of her want of vengeance, so a by the request rule
O my father, my country, that I have left to my shame; retelling of the departure at ev 2
after slaying my own brother; a killing; nothing later depends on it (Jason only cites it in reproach, S220), so it opens no move

This will I do; but I have my doubts whether I shall persuade my mistress; the Nurse agrees to act on the want
From the house I have come forth, Corinthian ladies, for fear lest you be blaming me; the Chorus's want is met; X also possible
this one boon and only this I wish to win from thee,— thy silence, if haply I can some way or means devise to avenge me; the hero's request, where the want of silence is first stated
This will I do; for thou wilt be taking a just vengeance on thy husband; help given, a means toward vengeance; the Chorus hears the plan (ev 39) and keeps silent

I bid thee take those sullen looks ... forth from this land in exile, and with thee take both thy children; a king's sentence of banishment taken as harm done (drives out); a by the request/demand rule and γ considered

let me abide in this land, for though I have been wronged I will be still; the hero's request, first statement of her want to stay; the promise is false (S058 "Dost think I would ever have fawned on yonder man, unless to gain some end"), η considered
Nay, begone at once! speak me no speeches, for this is decreed; help refused

yet shalt thou gain this request, lady; help given: the day in which she will act (S058 "he hath allowed me to abide this day, in which I will lay low in death three of my enemies"); θ considered, since Creon is deceived
if to-morrow's rising sun shall find thee and thy children within the borders of this land, thou diest; an order with a threat; never tested
in which I will lay low in death three of my enemies— a father and his daughter and my husband too ... by poison to destroy them; the hero decides to act

now for thy idle words wilt thou be banished; Jason comes and tells her the reason; nothing turns on it
Thou craven villain ... thou traitor! and thou hast cast me over; reproach to the wrongdoer
I saved thy life; Jason saved from destruction; N (solution) considered
when thou wert sent to tame and yoke fire-breathing bulls, and to sow the deadly tilth; a difficult task set; the sender is not named
I slew the dragon which guarded the golden fleece; the guardian killed
On thy house too maybe I bring the curse; a threat, carried out later; nearest A
if thou wilt of my fortune somewhat take ... yea and to send tokens to my friends elsewhere; an offer of help never received; nearest F (a helper offering service) or D
naught will I receive of thee, offer it not to me; refusal of the offer; nearest E or F−
go wed, for, if God will, thou shalt have such a marriage as thou wouldst fain refuse; a dismissal and a veiled threat or prophecy fulfilled at ev 57
All hail, Medea!; arrival of the man who will shelter her

He bade me not loose the wineskin's pendent neck; an oracle as command; nothing in the play fulfils it
receive me in thy country, to a seat within thy halls; the hero's request for refuge; she mused on this want in S058 ("What friendly host will give me a shelter") but first asks it here
I will make thy childlessness to cease and cause thee to beget fair issue; a helper offering service to Aegeus; a promise only, so X also possible

go call me Jason hither; an order, obeyed
No word divulge of all my purpose; an order of secrecy; nothing turns on it

ye, I trow, shall with your brothers share hereafter the foremost rank in this Corinthian realm; a promise never tested

these gifts as well which on a day my father's sire, the Sun-god, bestowed on his descendants; the agent the hero uses was given to her line

right glad were we thralls ... One kissed thy children's hands

Follow me, carrying the miserable burden of Pentheus, follow me, slaves, before the house
You father, receive them in your hands. Preening yourself in my catch, call your friends to a feast.
I have become somehow sobered, changing from my former state of mind; the madness of ev 9 lifted under Kadmos' questions
You gave me, as they say, to Echion, the sown man. "Pentheus, from my union with his father."; X, perhaps W
No, but I, wretched, hold the head of Pentheus.
You and your sisters killed him.; the killers made known
Dionysus destroyed us—now I understand.; X, perhaps Ex
That is what I, Dionysus, born not from a mortal father, but from Zeus, say.; the god shows himself, as vowed in ev 13; X, perhaps Q
changing your form, you will become a dragon ... You will sack many cities ... Ares will protect you; a prophecy beyond the play, answered by Kadmos' plea; X, perhaps T or U
Dionysus, we beseech you, we have acted injustly.; the want for mercy first stated
You have learned it too late; "My father Zeus approved this long ago."; the plea refused; F− applied to a request by one who is not the hero
Alas! A miserable exile has been decreed for us, old man.
O father, I will go into exile deprived of you. "Why do you embrace me with your hands, child"
Lead me, escorts, where I may take my pitiful sisters as companions to my exile; the sentence carried out; closes the play's action; X, perhaps ↑
Phoebus and I with exact measurement set towers of stone about this land of Troy and ringed it round; the building of the walls fulfills no function, and nothing later depends on it

Phocian Epeus, aided by the craft of Pallas, framed a horse to bear within its womb an armed army, and sent it within the battlements, a deadly statue; a deception to get inside the city, which leads to the slaughter

at the altar’s very base, before the god who watched his home, Priam lies dead; a killing. The performer is not named here; Hecuba later says "I saw their father, Priam, butchered on his own hearth" by the Greeks. First villainy, so it opens move I. Cassandra vows to "avenge my father’s and my brothers’ death"

smouldering and overthrown, a prey to Argive might ... to Achaean ships great store of gold and Phrygian spoils are being conveyed; the sack and plunder. Same harm toward the same end as ev 3 (the fall of Troy), so it stays in move I
Vanquished by Hera, Argive goddess, and by Athena, who helped to ruin Phrygia; the city's protecting god is beaten, which makes him leave; X, nearest I or A
I am leaving Ilium, that famous town, and my altars; the protector goes away. The sack is already done and he stays to plan with Athena, so nothing later depends on his leaving

the screams of captive maids, as they by lot receive their masters ... set apart for the leaders of the army; and with them Spartan Helen; carrying off the women as captives. Same harm toward the same end as ev 3 and ev 4, so no new move

at Achilles’ tomb, without her knowledge, her daughter Polyxena has died most piteously; a killing. The performer is not named; Andromache later says "slain at Achilles’ tomb, an offering". A new harm, a death rather than enslavement, so it opens move II

Cassandra ... has been forced by Agamemnon, in contempt of the god’s ordinance and of piety, to a dishonored wedlock; forced concubinage. Taken as the same harm as the captives "set apart for the leaders" (ev 7), so no new move. It could be read as a new villainy
if Pallas, daughter of Zeus, had not decreed your ruin, you would be standing firmly still; a decree. The harm itself is the sack, so X, nearest A
on behalf of Troy, whose soil we tread, I have come to seek your mighty aid, to make it one with mine; a request where Athena's want is first stated, so a (request rule), nearest B. Opens move III

Do you not know the insult done to me and to the shrine I love? / "when Aias dragged away Cassandra by force"; harm to Athena, and to Cassandra. It causes Athena's revenge. A new villainy, so it opens move IV
the Achaeans did nothing, said nothing to him; an omission. Athena answers it: "For which cause I would join with you to do them harm"; X, nearest A
And yet it was by your mighty aid they sacked Ilium; the sack again, now with Athena's aid. Same harm repeated, so no new move. Nearest alternative F (the Greeks receive Athena's aid)

he promises to grant me his thunder-bolts to hurl on the Achaeans ... And you, for your part, make the Aegean strait to roar; a request whose want was stated before ("I would join with you to do them harm"), so X, nearest B. Zeus's promise of the bolts is not carried out in the play: nearest F

So shall it be, for this favor needs only a few words. I will vex the broad Aegean sea; he agrees to act, which answers ev 15. The storm itself is not shown in the play, so it could be X as an intention not carried out
You swift-prowed ships, rowed to sacred Ilium ... in quest of that hateful wife of Menelaus; the Greeks set out after Helen, whom Menelaus now comes to fetch
O misery! woe to us Trojan women ... Come out of the house, the Argives are preparing to return; coming out in fear

Oh! please do not bid the wild Cassandra leave her chamber ... for Argives to insult; the hero's want, first stated, so a. Nothing answers it and Cassandra comes out on her own, so N; it opens no move. Nearest γ
With trembling step, alas! I leave this tent of Agamemnon to learn of you, my royal mistress
I, Talthybius, now sent with a fresh message; an arrival that brings the news of the lot
The lot has decided your fates already / "Each warrior took his prize in turn"; enslavement by lot. Same harm as ev 7, so no new move
King Agamemnon has chosen her out for himself / "to share with him his stealthy love"; same harm as ev 9
She too was a chosen prize; Achilles’ son took her; same harm as ev 22
Odysseus, king of Ithaca, has taken you to be his slave; the hero is enslaved. Same harm as ev 22, so no new move
Go, servants, and bring Cassandra forth to me here at once; a demand whose want was stated before (ev 23), so X, nearest γ. The servants do not bring her out; she rushes out on her own
Bring the light, uplift and show its flame! ... O Hymen, lord of marriage!; she sings her own wedding hymn, which leads Hecuba to take the torch
Give up the torch to me ... Take in those torches, Trojan friends

For I will slay him and lay waste his home to avenge my father’s and my brothers’ death; a prophecy and threat not fulfilled in the play, so X, nearest A. Talthybius dismisses it (ev 33), but nothing is done because of it
has lost for what he hated most what most he prized, yielding to his brother for a woman’s sake ... the joy he had of his own children; harm to his own children. N, so it opens no move
And Paris married the daughter of Zeus; a marriage; Cassandra says "she was willing and not taken by force". The marriage is what Menelaus comes to undo. Nearest alternative A (the theft, ev 57)
As for Hector and his griefs ... he is dead and gone; the household's protector dies. Later: "Hector will not rise from the earth ... to bring you salvation"
I give your taunts against Argos and your praise of Troy to the winds ... Follow me now to the ships; a demand whose want was stated before (ev 23), so X, nearest γ
Apollo’s words ... declare that she shall die here? ... he shall drag out other ten and then come to his country all alone; a prophecy not fulfilled or acted on in the play
Base you are, and basely shall you be buried ... my corpse cast forth in nakedness to wild beasts; a prophecy not fulfilled in the play

Lead on at once ... Where is that general’s ship?; Hecuba later: "Cassandra was torn with brutal violence from my arms"; she is carried off. Same harm as ev 23. Tearing off the garlands fulfills no function
see how your mistress is sinking speechless to the ground!
Leave me, my maidens ... lying where I fell
All these have I seen slain by the spear of Hellas; Hecuba's sons, who are not in the cast. Same harm as the sack, so no new move. Hecuba later calls on her dead children
when Achaea’s sons left at our gates that horse ... with its trappings of gold and its freight of warriors; the trickery of ev 2, told again
drag this sacred image to the shrine of the Zeus-born maiden ... with songs of joy they took the fatal snare within; the victims are taken in and help the deceivers
forth from their ambush came the warrior-band ... Soon the altars ran with Phrygian blood; same harm as ev 3 and ev 4, so no new move. The chorus "fell a wretched captive" because of it
My Achaean masters are leading me away; carried off as captive. Same harm as ev 24

since the day that son of yours escaped death, he that for a hated bride brought destruction on the Trojan citadel; the ruin of Troy, same end as move I. His escape from death has no named performer: nearest Rs

Your daughter Polyxena is dead, slain at Achilles’ tomb; the news reaches Hecuba, who cannot act on it, so not B. It answers ev 8 ("without her knowledge"): "This is that riddle Talthybius long ago told me"
I alighted from the chariot, and covered her corpse with a mantle, and struck upon my breast
you took from my father’s house a spotless bride, yourself the first to make this maiden wife; a marriage; nothing later depends on it

honor your present master ... rear my Hector’s child to lend stout aid to Ilium ... our city yet be established; Hecuba's want, first stated, so a. The Greeks' decree (ev 50) is not caused by it, so N, and it opens no move. Nearest γ
They mean to slay your son; there is my hateful message to you; the harm is made known to someone who cannot act on it, so not B

So spoke Odysseus to the assembled Hellenes, and his word prevails / "He said they should not rear so brave a father’s son"; it causes the child's death. A new villainy, so it opens move V. The harm itself is done at ev 87
nor would I hear you rashly curse the Achaeans. For if you say anything to anger the army, this child will find no burial; an interdiction. The burial is granted later (ev 90 to ev 96)
You daughter of Tyndareus ... Destruction catch you!; a curse on Helen, not on the Achaeans, so not δ against ev 51 (nearest δ). Nothing follows from it
Take the child and bear him hence, hurl him down if you wish; she yields the child; nearest E or θ
mount the high coronal of your ancestral towers, there to draw your parting breath ... Take him away; carried off to his death, which carries out ev 50
[Exeunt Andromache and Talthybius with Astyanax.]; Andromache is led away as captive. Same harm as ev 43
you came ... to sack our city Ilium, in days gone by ... the bow ... to be the doom of Laomedon; an earlier sack. N, so it opens no move
a husband to give her children, from this land, whom once a chariot of gold spangled stars caught up and carried there; told as divine favour, not harm, so X, nearest A
to punish the man who from my house stole my wife, traitor to my hospitality; theft of a wife. A new villainy, so it opens move VI. Menelaus comes for Helen because of it
But he, by the gods’ will, has paid the penalty, ruined, and his country too, by the spear of Hellas; it answers ev 57
have granted to me to slay her, or, if I will, to spare and carry back with me to Argos; Helen is handed over. Nearest K (the stolen wife back in his hands) or F
I have come to bear that wretched woman away ... Ho! my servants, enter the tent, and drag her out to me; a demand whose want, to recover Helen, was stated before (ev 17), so X, nearest γ
I thank you, Menelaus, if you will slay that wife of yours. Yet shun the sight of her; the hero's want, first stated, so a. Opens move VII
I am taken with violence by your servants’ hands and brought before these tents; a seizure, nearest A
Hear her, Menelaus; let her not die for want of that, and let me answer her again; the hero's request, toward a want stated before (ev 61), so X
still, if she wishes to speak, she may. Yet I will grant her this because of your words; the answer to the hero's request. The help is a means toward the want, so F

Yet I will put my charges and yours over against each other; a plea whose want was stated before ("May I answer this decision, proving that my death ... will be unjust?"), so X. Nearest H, as it opens the contest
that woman was the author of these troubles by giving birth to Paris
old Priam ruined Troy and me, because he did not slay his child Alexander; a failure to act. Nearest Rs for Paris
This man was to judge the claims of three rival goddesses; so Pallas offered him ... Hera promised ... Cypris ... promised him this gift; Paris is put to a judgement by possible givers. Nearest M
Cypris won the day over the goddesses; his response to the test
With no small goddess at his side he came, my evil genius; he is led to what he seeks. Nearest F or ↑
you, villain, left him behind in your house, and sailed away from Sparta to the land of Crete; the household's protector goes away and leaves it unprotected
what thought led me to follow the stranger from your house, traitress to my country and my home?; Menelaus: "she, without constraint, left my palace". Same harm as ev 57, so no new move
when Paris died, and earth concealed his corpse

often they found me seeking to let myself down stealthily by cords from the battlements; an attempt not carried out, so X, nearest ↑ or Rs. Hecuba rebuts it: "you assert that you tried to let yourself down"
Deiphobus, that carried me off by force to be his wife against the will of Troy; N, so it opens no move
often I advised you saying, Get away, daughter ... I will belp you to steal away; an order, also an offer of help (nearest D)
But this was bitter to you; the order is not obeyed. Nearest E−

First I will take up the cause of those goddesses, and prove how she perverts the truth ... crown Hellas by slaying her; the hero and Helen in contest before Menelaus. The demand in it is X (the want was stated in ev 61)
Your thoughts coincide with mine ... Away to those who shall stone you; Helen is beaten in the contest. The stoning is not carried out, so not U
Oh, by your knees, I implore you ... forgive me!; a plea whose want was stated before
Do not betray your allies, whose death this woman caused ... I entreat you; the hero's request, toward a want stated before (ev 61)
to her I pay no heed. I bid my servants take her away, aboard the ship; nearest F (the answer to ev 80) or U
Oh never let her set foot within the same ship as you; the hero's request, toward a want stated before ("shun the sight of her", ev 61)

your wish shall be granted; she shall not set foot upon the same ship with me ... when she comes to Argos she shall die; the request is granted. It is a promise not carried out on stage, so nearest K or X
[Exit Menelaus, dragging Helen with him.]; the punishment begins but is not completed, so X, nearest U
Oh may the sacred blazing thunderbolt ... smite the ship of Menelaus; a prayer not fulfilled in the play
[Enter Talthybius and attendants, bearing the corpse of Astyanax on Hector’s shield.]
the corpse of Astyanax, whom the Danaids have cruelly slain by hurling him from the battlements; this carries out the villainy of ev 50, so no new move
Acastus, son of Pelias, has banished him from the realm; a banishment. A new villainy, so it opens move VIII. It causes Neoptolemus to leave in haste
Neoptolemus is already out at sea ... and with him goes Andromache; "her master’s haste prevented her from burying the child herself"; nearest ↓, ↑ or A

she begged her master leave to bury this poor dead child ... let her bury the child in it ... and to your hands commit the corpse; a request where her want is first stated, so a. Opens move IX. For Hecuba it is also nearest B
one toil however I have already spared you, for I crossed Scamander’s stream and bathed the corpse and cleansed its wounds; a helper's service toward the burial
Ah, mother, many a lock of my hair I will cut off for you, and to your tomb will lead my troops of friends; a promise not kept
About your body now I swathe this Phrygian robe of honor ... dear shield of Hector ... accept your crown; the decking asked for in ev 90. Nearest K
those arms that the crafty villain Odysseus won; nearest W
Your wounds in part I will bind up with bandages
Go, bury now in his poor tomb the dead, wreathed all duly ... [The corpse is carried off to burial.]; the want of ev 90 is met
No longer keep the fire-brand idle in your hands, but launch the flame; a demand whose want, the city's destruction, was stated and acted on before. Nearest γ
start for the Achaean ships ... And you, unhappy grey-haired lady, follow; a demand whose want was stated before (ev 25)
Come, let us rush into the flames, for to die with my country in its blazing ruin would be a noble death for me; an attempt not carried out, so X. Nearest δ against ev 98
Go, lead her away, make no delay, for you must deliver her into the hand of Odysseus; a demand whose want was stated before. Nearest Rs, since it keeps her from the flames
Ilium is ablaze; the homes of Pergamos and its towering walls are now one sheet of flame; same harm as the sack, so no new move
Hearken, my children ... I stretch my aged limbs upon the ground, and beat upon the earth with both my hands; a lament to no one who might act
I follow you and kneel, invoking from the nether world my hapless husband
I am being dragged and hurried away— ... To dwell beneath a master’s roof!; carrying off. Same harm as ev 25
Yes, it was the crash of the citadel; the end of the city, which closes the play's action. No performer; nearest A
away! to face the day that begins your slavery / "And yet let us advance to the Achaean fleet"; the hero leaves home. It closes the play

terrible threats of spilling his rival’s blood were uttered by each of them, if he should fail to win the girl; threat only, not carried out; nearest candidate A; it is what moves Tyndareus to exact the oath

the suitors should swear to each other ... whoever wins the child of Tyndareus for wife, they will assist that man, in case a rival takes her from his house; the suitors are bound to a duty; the oath is invoked at ev 5

he allowed his daughter to choose ... Her choice fell on Menelaus; nearest candidate W, but this is a wedding at the outset, before any move, and Menelaus is not the hero; it makes Menelaus the husband robbed at ev 4
finding Menelaus gone from home; the husband’s absence leaves Helen unprotected and enables the abduction; told as a circumstance of the abduction
carried Helen off, in mutual desire, to his steading on Ida; abduction; opens move I; the Hellenes gather because of it
Menelaus flew through Hellas, invoking the ancient oath exacted by Tyndareus and declaring the duty of helping the injured husband; the misfortune made known and the sworn men called to act
the Hellenes, brandishing their spears and donning their harness, came here to the narrow straits of Aulis; the expedition sets out; Agamemnon goes with them
they chose me to captain them all for the sake of Menelaus; the hero is sent to act; nearest other candidate W (rank given), chosen B by what it causes: as commander he is the one the oracle binds
we still remained at Aulis weatherbound; lack of a sailing wind; opens move II; liquidated at ev 81

he answered that we should sacrifice my own child Iphigenia to Artemis ... we would sail and sack the Phrygians’ capital if we sacrificed her, but if we did not, these things would not happen; a hard condition set for the voyage; candidates a (as the goddess’s demand, by the request rule) and F (as the answer to the leaders’ asking for help)

I commanded Talthybius with loud proclamation to disband the whole army, as I could never bear to slay my daughter; Agamemnon’s refusal of the task, undone at ev 10; candidates γ (an order given) and N−
my brother, bringing every argument to bear, persuaded me at last to face the crime; the hero urged to act on the lack; candidate C (Agamemnon’s consent, implied in the same clause)
bidding her despatch our daughter to me on the pretence of wedding Achilles ... inventing, as I did, a sham marriage for the maiden; false words to get hold of the girl
that which I then decided wrongly, I now rightly countermand again in this scroll; nearest candidate γ, but the countermand never reaches Clytemnestra; it is the letter Menelaus seizes
Tyndareus sent me that day to form part of your wife’s dowry and to wait upon the bride with loyalty; the old man’s loyalty to Clytemnestra is why he reveals the plot to her
Not to despatch your daughter ... by promise of your daughter’s hand to the son of the goddess, were bringing the maid here to be sacrificed; the old man learns the secret he later tells
Start then from the bolted gates, and if you meet the escort, start them back again; the old man ordered to turn back the escort; the errand is cut short at ev 18
Helen, whom Paris the herdsman carried off ... his gift from Aphrodite, when that queen of Cyprus entered beauty’s contest; background to the abduction already told
To the sandy beach of sea-coast Aulis I have come ... so that I might behold the army of the Achaeans

[as Menelaus wrests a letter from him.]; "he snatched your letter violently from my grasp"; the countermand is stolen, so the daughter comes; opens move III; "Menelaus snatched it from me, he who caused this trouble" (S259)
this staff of mine will be dabbling your head with blood before long; threat only; candidate A
Master, he is wronging me; he snatched your letter violently from my grasp; the harm made known to the hero, who takes it up
No, not till I have shown its contents to all the army; refusal to give back the letter, with a threat not carried out; nearest candidate H (the brothers’ contest)
Yes, I opened it and know to your sorrow the secret machinations of your heart; Menelaus gains knowledge of Agamemnon’s plan, on which his accusation rests
taking each man by the hand ... Then when you had secured the command, there came a change over your manners

Then the Danaids began demanding that you should send the fleet away ... And you would ask my counsel, What am I to do?; the army’s demand is its first-stated want (request rule); nothing depends on it, so it opens no move; Agamemnon’s asking is not first statement of his want and gets no entry
you turn round and have been caught casting your letter ... I am more sorry for our unhappy Hellas; accusation; nearest candidate H (verbal contest)
I will not slay my children, nor shall your interests be prospered by justice in your vengeance for a worthless wife; refusal; candidates E and N−
Go boast of your scepter, after betraying your own brother! while I will seek some different means and other friends; threat not carried out

I have come and bring you your daughter ... and her mother, your wife Clytemnestra, is with her; "the army knows already of your daughter’s arrival"; deceived by the letter, the mother has brought the girl; the army’s knowledge is part of what compels Agamemnon
I withdraw from my former proposals ... do not slay your child ... Let the army be disbanded and leave Aulis; candidates F (a helper offering service) and I (Agamemnon: "yours is the victory")

circumstances compel me to carry out the murderous sacrifice of my daughter; the hero commits to the act that will meet the lack of wind (move II), though written in move III as the move already begun
Take one precaution for me, Menelaus ... that Clytemnestra does not learn this; the hero’s request where this want is first stated; nothing depends on Menelaus’s part, so no new move
And you, foreign women, keep silence; the chorus keeps the order and nothing turns on it; the secret is betrayed by the old man, who was not ordered
it is to a happy marriage I conduct the bride ... My daughter, leave the horse-drawn chariot; the arrival already entered as θ at ev 28
[throwing herself into Agamemnon’s arms.] I see you, father, joyfully after a long time
You too have a voyage to make ... All alone, without father or mother ... you will be standing near the libations
after you have given me your hand and a kiss ... Go into the house
Zeus, and she bore Aeacus, the prince of Oenone
Peleus, who wedded the daughter of Nereus ... the gods celebrated the marriage feast of Peleus
Chiron brought him up, to prevent his learning the ways of the wicked
Such is the future husband of your daughter ... As soon as the full moon comes; false words keep up the sham marriage
Go to Argos, and take care of your unwedded daughters ... Obey.
No, by the goddess-queen of Argos!; she stays, and so meets Achilles and learns the truth
I will go, in spite of all, with Calchas the priest, to inquire the goddess’s good pleasure
Achilles, the son of Peleus, is at his gates seeking him ... my Myrmidons, while they are always pressing on me; brings Achilles face to face with Clytemnestra
give me your hand, a prelude to a happy marriage; acting on the deception; candidate θ, but she does not help the deceiver
Lady, I have never courted your daughter, nor have the sons of Atreus ever mentioned marriage to me; the sham is found out but not its author; candidate Ex

Her father, he that begot her, is on the point of slaying your daughter with his own hand ... An inducement to you to bring your daughter cheerfully; the coming harm made known to those who will act on it; candidate Ex (the plan exposed)
Menelaus snatched it from me, he who caused this trouble; retells ev 18

Oh! help me, goddess-born, in my sore distress ... if you boldly stretch forth your arm in my behalf, our safety is assured; her want, her daughter’s safety, first stated here; by the request rule a lack; opens move IV
never shall king Agamemnon touch your daughter ... may I die, but live if I preserve the girl; Achilles agrees to act against the harm; candidate F (helper offering service)
Supplicate him first not to slay his children; and if he is stubborn, come to me ... I will keep watch to guard you; advice and a promise; candidates γ and F
Daughter of Nereus, you shall bear a son ... to set it in a blaze; no later event in the play fulfills it
my poor child, hearing of the death her father designs for her, is in tears
Send the maiden out to join her father ... heifers to be slain before the marriage, in honor of the goddess Artemis; still the pretence of marriage, to get the girl
Come forth, my daughter; well you know what is in your father’s mind; not taken in; she brings the girl out to plead
Ruined! my secret betrayed!; "Your very silence and those frequent groans are a confession"; the deceiver exposed to his face
by force that you took and wed me, after slaying Tantalus, my former husband, and dashing my baby on the ground; past villainy; nothing later depends on it, so no new move
those two sons of Zeus, who were my brothers, came flashing on horseback to war with you; candidates Pr and H
Tyndareus, my old father, rescued you because of your suppliant prayers; saved from destruction
and you in turn had me to wife
do not still slay your child, who is mine too ... give you the reception it is right you should receive; a plea whose want was stated before (ev 48), and a threat not carried out; candidate D
By Pelops, I entreat you spare me ... entreat our father for your sister’s life; the same want toward the same end; candidates a and D
it is Hellas, for whom I must sacrifice you whether I will or not; the hero refuses the plea; no D was written before it
where Priam once exposed a tender baby, torn from his mother’s arms to meet a deadly doom; past harm; nothing depends on it
A fearful cry is heard among the Argives ... They say her sacrifice is necessary; demand already stated
Of being stoned ... They were the first who turned against me; threat not carried out; Iphigenia’s resolve answers it
But I will help you for all that ... Do you see these warriors here, carrying my arms?; a promise only, repeating ev 49; candidate C
I am resolved to die ... I give my body to Hellas; sacrifice it and make an utter end of Troy; she agrees to act against the army’s lack; candidate E
how I grieve to think I shall not save your life by doing battle with the Danaids; offer refused; candidate F
be not slain yourself, stranger, nor seek to slay another on my account
I will go and place these arms of mine near the altar ... await your arrival there; the arms are never used
Cut not off the tresses of your hair for me ... promise me to rear Orestes ... do not hate my father; nothing later depends on it
let one of these attendants of my father conduct me to the meadow of Artemis, where I shall be sacrificed; a request toward the end already stated at ev 66; candidates a and G
May it be yours, maidens, to hymn ... let the order for a solemn hush go forth to the Danaids. Begin the sacrifice
A different life, a different lot is henceforth mine. Farewell I bid you, light beloved! [Exit Iphigenia.]; she sets out for the altar
As soon as we reached the grove of Artemis ... bringing your daughter with us, at once the Argive army began assembling; candidate G
he gave one groan, and, turning away his face, let the tears burst from his eyes
willingly I offer my body for my country and all Hellas ... let none of the Argives lay hands on me; repeats ev 66
bade the army refrain from word or deed
drawing a sharp sword from its scabbard laid it in a basket of beaten gold, and crowned the maiden’s head
accept this sacrifice ... and grant us safe sailing for our ships; a want stated before
the priest, seizing his knife ... Each one of us distinctly heard the sound of a blow; the sacrifice set at ev 8 is performed
none saw the spot where the maiden vanished ... there upon the ground lay a deer; "due to some god’s agency"; the girl saved from death; candidate K (Clytemnestra’s want at ev 48 met)
Gladly she has accepted it, and is granting us a prosperous voyage ... today we must leave the hollow bays of Aulis; the lack of wind (ev 7) set right
when the sacrifice was wholly burnt to ashes ... he offered such prayers as were fitting, that the army might win return
Agamemnon sends me to tell you this
without a doubt your child flew away to the gods
she has fellowship with gods. But you must take this tender child and start for home
the army is looking now to sail. Fare you well! it is long before I shall greet you on my return from Troy; the hero sets out; closes the play’s action

He ought to receive fresh tidings from the warriors who were set to guard the assembled army; "It is time to hearken."; the guards rouse Hector to act on news; B, though the misfortune itself is only told in ev 2

the Argive army has kindled fires, and bright with torches shines the anchored fleet; the fires are what Hector answers, but no function names an enemy's fires; nearest candidate B (the report), already written at ev 1
nor ever before did they suffer such shameful defeat and rout; combat won by Hector; nearest candidate I (driven off), but the enemy is not ended and the war goes on, so H

a mind unstable is an unjust possession, disloyal to friends ... "I am more sorry for our unhappy Hellas"; Menelaus attacks him and later gives help; nearest alternative X
I will not slay my children; he withstands
while I will seek some different means and other friends; threat not carried out; candidate A
I have come and bring you your daughter, whom you call Iphigenia in your home ... "the army knows already of your daughter’s arrival"; X; announcement; the arrival itself is entered at ev 32
I withdraw from my former proposals, ceasing to be a cause of fear to you ... "Let the army be disbanded and leave Aulis"; help offered; nearest alternative X
circumstances compel me to carry out the murderous sacrifice of my daughter; he decides to act
Take one precaution for me, Menelaus, as you go through the army, that Clytemnestra does not learn this; request for help, want of secrecy stated before; candidate a
And you, foreign women, keep silence.; order to the chorus
have good hope that it is to a happy marriage I conduct the bride; taken in by the deception, she brings the victim
[throwing herself into Agamemnon’s arms.] I see you, father, joyfully after a long time.; X
You too have a voyage to make to a haven where you will remember your father. ... "All alone, without father or mother."; veiled words, not false; candidate η
Go within—it is wrong for maidens to be seen—after you have given me your hand and a kiss; order to go in; the kiss is no function
Zeus, and she bore Aeacus, the prince of Oenone; X; genealogy, candidate W
Peleus, who wedded the daughter of Nereus; X; candidate W
Chiron brought him up, to prevent his learning the ways of the wicked.; X
Such is the future husband of your daughter.; false words continue the deception
Go to Argos, and take care of your unwedded daughters.; order
No, by the goddess-queen of Argos! ... "in the house it is my place to decide what is proper for maidens at their wedding"; order not obeyed
But I will go, in spite of all, with Calchas the priest, to inquire the goddess’s good pleasure; X; nothing depends on it
Where is Achaea’s general? Which of his servants will announce to him that Achilles, the son of Peleus, is at his gates seeking him?; X; his arrival makes the discovery possible
give me your hand, a prelude to a happy marriage; X, nearest candidate θ; she acts on the false belief but does not help the villain
Lady, I have never courted your daughter, nor have the sons of Atreus ever mentioned marriage to me.; the pretence is exposed
Her father, he that begot her, is on the point of slaying your daughter with his own hand.; the misfortune is made known
Menelaus snatched it from me, he who caused this trouble.; X; repeats ev 18
Oh! help me, goddess-born, in my sore distress; first statement of her want that the girl be saved; opens move IV
I will not tell a lie; if I do that or idly mock you, may I die, but live if I preserve the girl.; help given in answer
Supplicate him first not to slay his children; and if he is stubborn, come to me.; she is sent to act
I will keep watch to guard you, where occasion calls; further offer of help
you shall bear a son, a dazzling light to Thessaly ... "to set it in a blaze"; prophecy; nothing in this play fulfills it
my poor child, hearing of the death her father designs for her, is in tears; X, nearest candidate B
Send the maiden out to join her father; order
Come forth, my daughter; X; she complies in order to confront him
Your very silence and those frequent groans are a confession ... "Ruined! my secret betrayed!"; the villain is exposed
after slaying Tantalus, my former husband; past killing
dashing my baby on the ground when you had torn him from my breast with brutal violence; past killing of the infant
it was not of my own free will but by force that you took and wed me; past carrying off
those two sons of Zeus, who were my brothers, came flashing on horseback to war with you; nearest alternative X
Tyndareus, my old father, rescued you because of your suppliant prayers; the gift of Clytemnestra is no further function
do not still slay your child, who is mine too, and you will be wise ... "give you the reception it is right you should receive"; plea after want stated at ev 48; warning is a threat not carried out
Do not destroy me before my time ... "By Pelops, I entreat you spare me"; plea; want stated before
it is Hellas, for whom I must sacrifice you whether I will or not; refusal of the plea; nearest candidates C or F−
where Priam once exposed a tender baby, torn from his mother’s arms to meet a deadly doom, Paris; past exposure; nothing depends on it
They say her sacrifice is necessary.; demand already stated at ev 8; candidate γ
Of being stoned. ... "They were the first who turned against me."; threat not carried out; candidate H
But I will help you for all that.; he decides to act
I am resolved to die ... "I give my body to Hellas; sacrifice it and make an utter end of Troy."; she decides to act
Look to it; for I want to serve you and receive you in my halls; offer of help, refused at ev 68; candidate F
a fond desire to win you for my bride; want of a mate; nothing depends on it
then be not slain yourself, stranger, nor seek to slay another on my account; offered help refused; nearest alternative X
I will go and place these arms of mine near the altar, resolved not to permit your death but to prevent; X; conditional intent, nothing later depends on it
promise me to rear Orestes to manhood ... "do not hate my father, your own husband"; several commands taken as one entry
Be persuaded by me, mother, stay here; order
and let the order for a solemn hush go forth to the Danaids. Begin the sacrifice with the baskets; order
Farewell I bid you, light beloved! [Exit Iphigenia.]; she sets out to the sacrifice
As soon as we reached the grove of Artemis, the child of Zeus ... "at once the Argive army began assembling"; X, nearest candidate G
he gave one groan, and, turning away his face, let the tears burst from his eyes; X
willingly I offer my body for my country and all Hellas; offers the means to the sacrifice
So then let none of the Argives lay hands on me; interdiction, not broken
Talthybius stood up, for this was his duty, and bade the army refrain from word or deed; order
Calchas, the seer, drawing a sharp sword from its scabbard laid it in a basket of beaten gold, and crowned the maiden’s head; rite; the sacrifice is not carried out
accept this sacrifice which we, the army of the Achaeans and Agamemnon with us, offer to you ... "grant us safe sailing for our ships"; request after want stated before; answered at ev 81
none saw the spot where the maiden vanished ... "there upon the ground lay a deer of immense size"; victim freed; nearest alternative Rs
Gladly she has accepted it, and is granting us a prosperous voyage for our attack on Ilium.; the want of passage is met
away to your ships; order
Then, when the sacrifice was wholly burnt to ashes in the blazing flame, he offered such prayers as were fitting, that the army might win return; X
Agamemnon sends me to tell you this; order
your child flew away to the gods; X; report that closes her lack
But you must take this tender child and start for home; order
for the army is looking now to sail; he sets out for Troy
But them Sky bound and cast into Tartarus; imprisonment of his own children (form 15, imprisons or detains). A harmful act by the hero, judged like any other.

Earth, grieved at the destruction of her children, who had been cast into Tartarus, persuaded the Titans to attack their father; X, perhaps B². The act is a dispatch, but B is the dispatch of the hero, and those dispatched here are the hero's opponents.
gave Cronus an adamantine sickle; X, perhaps F¹. F is the hero's receipt of an agent; here the agent goes to the hero's opponent.
And they, all but Ocean, attacked him; struggle between the hero and his opponents; form not named.

Cronus cut off his father's genitals and threw them into the sea; the hero loses the fight. Sky is also the one who committed the villainy of ev 1, so the same act is I in the Cronus transcription. Throwing the genitals into the sea fulfills no function and has no entry.
having dethroned their father; punishment of the one who committed the villainy of ev 1; perhaps X, since the text does not link the dethronement to the imprisonment.
But them Sky bound and cast into Tartarus; the Cyclopes are Cronus's brothers; imprisonment (form 15).

Earth, grieved at the destruction of her children, who had been cast into Tartarus, persuaded the Titans to attack their father; the misfortune is the ground of the request, and the hero is dispatched directly by persuasion (B²). No separate decision (C) is told.
gave Cronus an adamantine sickle; agent directly transferred; it is used in ev 5.
And they, all but Ocean, attacked him; struggle; form not named.
Cronus cut off his father's genitals and threw them into the sea; the villain defeated; form not named (a maiming, not a fight in open field). Throwing the genitals into the sea has no entry.
having dethroned their father; punishment of the villain; perhaps X, since the text does not link the dethronement to the imprisonment.
they brought up their brethren who had been hurled down to Tartarus; captives freed. The imprisonment it undoes is told in L1-001, outside this episode.
and committed the sovereignty to Cronus; accession to the throne only (Propp's third form of W); bare W, since the extracted text's sign for that form is not legible.
But he again bound and shut them up in Tartarus; imprisonment (form 15). The first villainy of the episode, so it stays in move I.

since both Earth and Sky foretold him that he would be dethroned by his own son; X, perhaps ζ. The prophecy motivates the villainy of ev 5, but it is a warning, not information about a victim sought by the villain.

undergoer: his children Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Pluto, Poseidon
note: he used to swallow his offspring at birth. His firstborn Hestia he swallowed, then Demeter and Hera, and after them Pluto and Poseidon; bare A. Swallowing alive falls between detention (15) and cannibalism (17, which Propp lists only as a threat).

Enraged at this, Rhea repaired to Crete, when she was big with Zeus; X, perhaps C and ↑, but the act is Rhea's, not the hero's. The swallowing that enrages her is told in L1-002 and is not entered here.
brought him forth in a cave of Dicte; the hero's birth introduces him (initial situation, which Propp calls a morphological element, not a function).

She gave him to the Curetes and to the nymphs Adrastia and Ida, daughters of Melisseus, to nurse; X, perhaps B⁶ (a child condemned to death secretly saved), but the text does not say here that she saves him from anyone.
So these nymphs fed the child on the milk of Amalthea.

the Curetes in arms guarded the babe in the cave, clashing their spears on their shields in order that Cronus might not hear the child's voice; X, perhaps Rs⁴ (the hero hidden), but there is no pursuit.

Rhea wrapped a stone in swaddling clothes and gave it to Cronus to swallow, as if it were the newborn child; X, perhaps η. It is a deception, but practised on the villain to save the hero, not by a villain to take possession of a victim.
when Zeus was full-grown, he took Metis, daughter of Ocean, to help him; the hero acquires a helper; form not named (she is neither given, found, nor said to offer herself).
she gave Cronus a drug to swallow; X, perhaps η² (a potion administered) or part of the liquidation whose result is ev 9.
which forced him to disgorge first the stone and then the children whom he had swallowed; the captives freed. The swallowing it undoes is told in L1-002.
with their aid Zeus waged the war against Cronus and the Titans; struggle with an enemy army. The aid of the brothers and sisters is a circumstance, not a separate act.
They fought for ten years; the duration of the struggle of ev 10; no new act.

Earth prophesied victory to Zeus if he should have as allies those who had been hurled down to Tartarus; X, perhaps F² (helpers pointed out) or a (a need for helpers felt in mid-course, as Propp describes on p.95).
So he slew their jailoress Campe; X, perhaps I⁵. The slaying serves the freeing of ev 14.
and loosed their bonds; the hero frees captives, and a gift follows (ev 15), which Propp gives as what separates this from K¹⁰ (p.55).
the Cyclopes then gave Zeus thunder and lightning and a thunderbolt, and on Pluto they bestowed a helmet and on Poseidon a trident; agents directly transferred.
Armed with these weapons the gods overcame the Titans; beaten in open combat.
shut them up in Tartarus, and appointed the Hundred-handers their guards; the appointing of guards has no entry.
they themselves cast lots for the sovereignty, and to Zeus was allotted the dominion of the sky; accession to the throne only; bare W.
Menoetius, he whom Zeus in the battle with the Titans smote with a thunderbolt; flashback, told in a genealogy after the war is over; form not named.
and hurled down to Tartarus; flashback; the same punishment as ev 17.

Zeus caused oaths to be sworn by the water of Styx ... bestowing this honor on her because she and her children had fought on his side against the Titans; a reward to a helper, no function. The helpers' fighting is a flashback inside the struggle already entered at ev 10.
when his wife Eurydice died, bitten by a snake; killing by a figure told of only in passing; perhaps to be read instead as a lack of a wife (a¹).
being fain to bring her up; the decision to counteract, expressed in words.
he went down to Hades; departure. The descent to another kingdom is its natural continuation, so G is not singled out (p.51).
he persuaded Pluto to send her up; X, perhaps K³ (obtained by enticement), but the release is only promised and is never completed.
The god promised to do so, if on the way Orpheus would not turn round until he should be come to his own house; interdiction.
But he disobeyed and turning round beheld his wife; violation.

performer: Eurydice, as a result of Orpheus's violation
note: so she turned back; a disappearance brought about by the hero's own act, as in Propp's tale 267 under A⁷; perhaps a negative liquidation (K−) rather than a new villainy.
Orpheus also invented the mysteries of Dionysus.
having been torn in pieces by the Maenads; murder; nothing follows in the episode.
Him Zeus cast out of heaven; expulsion.
because he came to the rescue of Hera in her bonds; flashback, told as the reason for ev 1; X, perhaps C or K¹⁰. The text does not say whether he freed her.
when Hercules had taken Troy and was at sea; flashback.
Hera sent a storm after him; flashback; harm to a figure told of only in passing; form not named. Move I breaks off here.
so Zeus hung her from Olympus; flashback. The act is also a reprisal for ev 4 (perhaps U); defined by its consequence, Hephaestus's attempt to rescue "Hera in her bonds" (ev 2), it is a detention.
Hephaestus fell on Lemnos and was lamed of his legs; the flashback ends and move I resumes here; the fall completes the expulsion of ev 1. X, perhaps A⁶ for the laming.
but Thetis saved him; X, perhaps K or Rs. The text does not say from what she saved him.
Zeus had intercourse with Metis; X, perhaps A. The union is against her will (ev 2), but Propp lists only the threat of forced marriage (A¹⁶).
who turned into many shapes in order to avoid his embraces; X, perhaps Rs⁶ (escape by rapid transformations), but she does not escape, and she is not the hero.
because Earth said that, after giving birth to the maiden who was then in her womb, Metis would bear a son who should be the lord of heaven; X, perhaps ζ, as in L1-002 ev 4.
From fear of that Zeus swallowed her; also "When she was with child, Zeus, taking time by the forelock, swallowed her"; bare A, as in L1-002 ev 5. A harmful act by the hero.
when the time came for the birth to take place, Prometheus or, as others say, Hephaestus, smote the head of Zeus with an axe; the delivery of a birth.
Athena, fully armed, leaped up from the top of his head at the river Triton; X, perhaps K (the swallowed child released, as in L1-003 ev 9), but the text tells it as a birth, not a rescue.
Apollo learned the art of prophecy from Pan; a capacity directly given (Propp's fourth class of agents). It is not used against an adversary in the text.
came to Delphi, where Themis at that time used to deliver oracles; X, perhaps G; no search is declared.
when the snake Python, which guarded the oracle, would have hindered him from approaching the chasm; X, perhaps H. The hindering is told only as an attempt ("would have").
he killed it; the adversary defeated; form not named, since the text does not say whether a fight preceded.
and took over the oracle; obtained as the direct result of the victory. No lack is told.
for her, after he had debauched her; flashback inside the account of Tityus; X, perhaps A.
Zeus hid under the earth for fear of Hera; flashback.
brought forth to the light the son Tityus, of monstrous size; flashback.
When Latona came to Pytho; the hero's mother away from home, the occasion of the villainy that follows.
Tityus beheld her, and overpowered by lust drew her to him; assault on the hero's mother; form not named. The first villainy of the episode, so it stays in move I.
But she called her children to her aid; a call for help.
they shot him down with their arrows; killed without a preliminary fight.
he is punished even after death; for vultures eat his heart in Hades.
the pipes which Athena had thrown away because they disfigured her face; flashback.
Marsyas, having found the pipes; X, perhaps F⁵, but the finder is the hero's opponent.
engaged in a musical contest with Apollo; competition.
They agreed that the victor should work his will on the vanquished.
Apollo turned his lyre upside down in the competition and bade Marsyas do the same; a stroke within the contest of ev 16; X, perhaps M, but set to the opponent, not the hero.
But Marsyas could not; X, perhaps N− for the opponent.
so Apollo was judged the victor; defeated in a contest.
despatched Marsyas by hanging him on a tall pine tree and stripping off his skin; X, perhaps U. The text names no offence, only the terms agreed at ev 17.
Poseidon bestowed on him the power of striding across the sea; a capacity directly given; not used later in the episode.
He first married Side, whom Hera cast into Hades because she rivalled herself in beauty; harm to the hero's wife; form not named (killing, or expulsion to the underworld).
Afterwards he went to Chios; departure; no search is stated.
wooed Merope, daughter of Oenopion; desire for a bride; a new lack, so move II begins.
But Oenopion made him drunk; form not named (Propp's sleeping potion is η², but the wine is not said to be magical; otherwise η³).
as he slept; the victim reacts mechanically to the means of ev 5 by falling asleep; told only as the circumstance of the blinding.
put out his eyes as he slept; bodily injury (Propp's example is the cutting out of eyes).
and cast him on the beach; expulsion. A second harmful act, so by the rule it begins move IV; move III breaks off here.
But he went to the smithy of Hephaestus; move III resumes here, since the journey is the quest for his sight; departure of a victimized hero.
snatching up a lad set him on his shoulders; a helper seized.
and bade him lead him to the sunrise; the hero is led.
Being come thither he was healed by the sun's rays, and having recovered his sight; the injury of ev 6 undone; form not in Propp's list.
he hastened with all speed against Oenopion; X, perhaps ↑ or C. The vengeance is intended and never carried out.
But for him Poseidon had made ready a house under the earth constructed by Hephaestus; flashback; X, perhaps Rs⁴ (hiding), but it shelters the opponent.
And Dawn fell in love with Orion; X, perhaps a (Dawn's desire), but the desire leads to her harming him, not to a quest.
and carried him off and brought him to Delos; abduction.
for Aphrodite caused Dawn to be perpetually in love; flashback, told as a reason; X, perhaps A¹¹ (a spell) or U (on Dawn, for ev 16).
because she had bedded with Ares; flashback.
for challenging Artemis to a match at quoits; told as the reason for ev 18; X, perhaps H², but only the challenge is told, not a contest.
And Artemis slew Orion in Delos; "Orion was killed, as some say, for challenging Artemis"; the killing is given as retribution for ev 17; perhaps A¹⁴.

Demeter went about seeking her all over the earth with torches by night and day; departure on a search. The decision (C) is not told apart from the search. The abduction ("carried her off secretly") is told before the episode begins.

learning from the people of Hermion that Pluto had carried her off; the misfortune announced by persons met by chance. The abduction reported here is a census event outside this episode and is not entered again.
she was wroth with the gods and quitted heaven; departure from home; perhaps X.
came in the likeness of a woman to Eleusis; unrecognized arrival.
first she sat down on the rock which has been named Laughless after her, beside what is called the Well of the Fair Dances.
thereupon she made her way to Celeus, who at that time reigned over the Eleusinians; continuation of the arrival of ev 4.
when they bade her sit down beside them; X, perhaps D² (a greeting), but nothing is given to her.
a certain old crone, Iambe, joked the goddess and made her smile.
Metanira, wife of Celeus, had a child and Demeter received it to nurse; X, perhaps part of o (the hero arrived unrecognized takes service).
wishing to make it immortal she set the babe of nights on the fire and stripped off its mortal flesh; X, perhaps T or F for the child. The immortality is intended and not achieved.
Demophon ... grew marvelously by day.
Praxithea watched, and discovering him buried in the fire she cried out; X, perhaps δ, but no interdiction is told.
wherefore the babe was consumed by the fire; X, perhaps A¹⁴; no one is said to intend the death.
and the goddess revealed herself; recognition after the unrecognized arrival of ev 4, brought about by her own revelation.
for Triptolemus, the elder of Metanira's children, she made a chariot of winged dragons, and gave him wheat; X, perhaps F³ and F¹, but the recipient is not the hero; one X for the event.
with which, wafted through the sky, he sowed the whole inhabited earth.
when Zeus ordered Pluto to send up the Maid; the abduction undone by command; the return is only partial (ev 22).
Pluto gave her a seed of a pomegranate to eat, in order that she might not tarry long with her mother; an object offered for acceptance (Propp's ring to be accepted).
Not foreseeing the consequence, she swallowed it.
because Ascalaphus, son of Acheron and Gorgyra, bore witness against her; X, perhaps ζ; the one who receives the testimony is not named.
Demeter laid a heavy rock on him in Hades; punishment of the one whose testimony harmed Persephone.

Persephone was compelled to remain a third of every year with Pluto and the rest of the time with the gods; X. The arrangement is at once a detention (A¹⁵) and a partial return (K), and no consequence follows to decide it, since the episode ends here.
Earth, vexed on account of the Titans, brought forth the giants, whom she had by Sky; the heroes' birth introduces them.
And they darted rocks and burning oaks at the sky; war on the gods (Propp's example: a dragon ravages kingdoms). The first villainy of the episode, so it stays in move I.
He also drove away the cows of the Sun from Erythia; plunder; nothing follows from it in the episode.
Learning of this, Earth sought for a simple to prevent the giants from being destroyed even by a mortal; a magical agent needed; the learning of the oracle has no entry of its own.

But Zeus forbade the Dawn and the Moon and the Sun to shine; the darkness keeps Earth from the herb, like Propp's dragon who rearranges the shavings that show the way (η³). Perhaps A⁴ (seizure of daylight), which it resembles in form.
and then, before anybody else could get it, he culled the simple himself; X, perhaps A², but the agent was only sought by the heroes' side, not held.
by means of Athena summoned Hercules to his help; X, perhaps B¹ or F, but for the heroes' opponent.
Hercules first shot Alcyoneus with an arrow; struggle.
when the giant fell on the ground he somewhat revived; X, perhaps K⁹.
at Athena's advice Hercules dragged him outside Pallene.
and so the giant died; the hero's side loses.
But in the battle Porphyrion attacked Hercules and Hera.
Nevertheless Zeus inspired him with lust for Hera; direct application of magical means by the heroes' opponent.
when he tore her robes and would have forced her; the tearing is done, the forcing only intended; harm to Hera; form not named. Perhaps θ instead (the reaction to ev 13).
she called for help; X, perhaps B¹, but those called are the heroes' opponents.
Zeus smote him with a thunderbolt; a blow in the struggle, not the defeat; perhaps I−.
Hercules shot him dead with an arrow.
Ephialtes was shot by Apollo with an arrow in his left eye and by Hercules in his right.
Eurytus was killed by Dionysus with a thyrsus.
and Clytius by Hecate with torches.
and Mimas by Hephaestus with missiles of red-hot metal.
Enceladus fled; X, perhaps the beginning of a rescue (Rs), which fails.
but Athena threw on him in his flight the island of Sicily; perhaps Pr.
and she flayed Pallas and used his skin to shield her own body in the fight; the use of the skin has no entry.
Polybotes was chased through the sea by Poseidon and came to Cos; pursuit; form not named.
Poseidon, breaking off that piece of the island which is called Nisyrum, threw it on him.
Hermes, wearing the helmet of Hades, slew Hippolytus in the fight.
and Artemis slew Gration.
the Fates, fighting with brazer clubs, killed Agrius and Thoas.
The other giants Zeus smote and destroyed with thunderbolts.
all of them Hercules shot with arrows as they were dying; X, perhaps I− (the mortal's share foretold by the oracle of ev 4); the deaths are already entered.
Earth, still more enraged, had intercourse with Tartarus and brought forth Typhon in Cilicia; the hero's birth introduces him.
hurling kindled rocks, he made for the very heaven with hissings and shouts, spouting a great jet of fire from his mouth; war on heaven.
when the gods saw him rushing at heaven, they made for Egypt in flight.
and being pursued they changed their forms into those of animals; X, perhaps Pr and Rs⁶, but those pursued are not the hero; one X for the event.
However Zeus pelted Typhon at a distance with thunderbolts; struggle.
and at close quarters struck him down with an adamantine sickle; a blow within the struggle; X, perhaps J¹ (a wound in the fight) or I−. Typhon is not defeated; he flees and fights on.
and as he fled pursued him closely as far as Mount Casius; pursuit; form not named.
seeing the monster sore wounded, he grappled with him.
But Typhon twined about him and gripped him in his coils; the hero overcomes his adversary; form not named.

wresting the sickle from him severed the sinews of his hands and feet; bodily injury. The sinews are then carried off and hidden (ev 12), the seizure that Propp notes under A⁶. The wresting of the sickle has no entry.

lifting him on his shoulders carried him through the sea to Cilicia and deposited him on arrival in the Corycian cave; a second harmful act, which by the rule begins move III; perhaps A¹ (abduction). Move II breaks off here.
Likewise he put away the sinews there also, hidden in a bearskin.
he set to guard them the she-dragon Delphyne, who was a half-bestial maiden.
But Hermes and Aegipan stole the sinews and fitted them unobserved to Zeus; move II resumes here: the injury of ev 10 undone by stealth. The theft and the fitting are entered as one liquidation.
having recovered his strength Zeus suddenly from heaven, riding in a chariot of winged horses, pelted Typhon with thunderbolts.
and pursued him to the mountain called Nysa.
where the Fates beguiled the fugitive; persuasion.
for he tasted of the ephemeral fruits in the persuasion that he would be strengthened thereby.
So being again pursued he came to Thrace.
and in fighting at Mount Haemus he heaved whole mountains.
But when these recoiled on him through the force of the thunderbolt; the hero loses.
a stream of blood gushed out on the mountain.
And when he started to flee through the Sicilian sea; X, perhaps the beginning of a rescue (Rs), which fails.
Zeus cast Mount Etna in Sicily upon him; overthrown in flight, entered as Enceladus in L1-020 ev 23; perhaps U.
Prometheus moulded men out of water and earth.
and gave them also fire; X, perhaps F¹, but the recipients are not the hero.
which, unknown to Zeus, he had hidden in a stalk of fennel; flashback; the text later names it "the theft of fire"; plunder. A harmful act by the hero.
But when Zeus learned of it; X, perhaps Ex.
he ordered Hephaestus to nail his body to Mount Caucasus; the order; its execution (ev 6) is entered as the harm.

On it Prometheus was nailed and kept bound for many years; imprisonment. The text calls it a penalty ("That was the penalty that Prometheus paid for the theft of fire"), that is U; its consequence, the release by Hercules (ev 8), marks it as a misfortune later undone.
Every day an eagle swooped on him and devoured the lobes of his liver, which grew by night; a repeated torment, nearest A¹⁸ (torment at night); form not named.
until Hercules afterwards released him; captive freed. It ends the imprisonment of move II as well (a common ending).
Deucalion by the advice of Prometheus constructed a chest; the means of rescue prepared on a donor's advice; form between F² and F³; perhaps X.
having stored it with provisions he embarked in it with Pyrrha; departure; the storing has no entry.

But Zeus by pouring heavy rain from heaven flooded the greater part of Greece; the destruction of a people; form not named (nearest A¹⁹, ravaging). The earlier "when Zeus would destroy the men of the Bronze Age" is intention only.
so that all men were destroyed, except a few who fled to the high mountains in the neighborhood; the result of ev 3.
the mountains in Thessaly parted, and ... all the world outside the Isthmus and Peloponnese was overwhelmed.
floating in the chest over the sea for nine days and as many nights, drifted to Parnassus; X, perhaps G², but there is no object of search.
when the rain ceased, he landed.
