she told him to dwell in Tiryns, serving Eurystheus for twelve years and to perform the ten labours imposed on him, and so, she said, when the tasks were accomplished, he would be immortal; sent by command, with a promise; perhaps γ² (an order) or M
he went to Tiryns and did as he was bid by Eurystheus; leaves for his appointed dwelling; perhaps X
Eurystheus ordered him to bring the skin of the Nemean lion; a task of supply
he came to Cleonae and lodged at the house of a day-laborer, Molorchus

Hercules told him to wait for thirty days, and then, if he had returned safe from the hunt, to sacrifice to Saviour Zeus, but if he were dead, to sacrifice to him as to a hero; X, perhaps γ² (an order)
having come to Nemea and tracked the lion, he first shot an arrow at him; the combat begins
he heaved up his club and made after him; continues the struggle already entered at ev 22
the lion took refuge in a cave with two mouths
Hercules built up the one entrance and came in upon the beast through the other; part of the struggle
putting his arm round its neck held it tight till he had choked it; outcome of the combat. The task was to bring the skin, so the kill is entered as I and the delivery (ev 29) as N
laying it on his shoulders he carried it to Cleonae; the way back begins
finding Molorchus on the last of the thirty days about to sacrifice the victim to him as to a dead man, he sacrificed to Saviour Zeus
brought the lion to Mycenae; the task is done

Eurystheus forbade him thenceforth to enter the city, but ordered him to exhibit the fruits of his labours before the gates; an interdiction together with its paired order, entered once; no violation follows in the text

As a second labour he ordered him to kill the Lernaean hydra; the next sentence, "used to go forth into the plain and ravage both the cattle and the country", describes the hydra and is not given as the reason for the order, so it gets no entry
mounting a chariot driven by Iolaus, he came to Lerna; sets out on the task; perhaps G² (carried by a helper's chariot)
he discovered the hydra on a hill beside the springs of the Amymone
By pelting it with fiery shafts he forced it to come out; the combat begins
he seized and held it fast; part of the struggle
the hydra wound itself about one of his feet and clung to him; part of the struggle
Nor could he effect anything by smashing its heads with his club; part of the struggle
A huge crab also came to the help of the hydra by biting his foot
So he killed it; X, perhaps I (over a second adversary within the same struggle)
in his turn called for help on Iolaus

by setting fire to a piece of the neighboring wood and burning the roots of the heads with the brands, prevented them from sprouting; the helper's act that makes the kill possible; X, perhaps part of N
he chopped off the immortal head, and buried it, and put a heavy rock on it; the task (to kill) is done
the body of the hydra he slit up and dipped his arrows in the gall; he makes himself poisoned arrows; the form is not certain (F³ made, F⁸ taken)
Eurystheus said that this labour should not be reckoned among the ten; the solution is refused; X, perhaps a negative N, which the rules do not list
As a third labour he ordered him to bring the Cerynitian hind alive to Mycenae
wishing neither to kill nor wound it, Hercules hunted it a whole year
weary with the chase, the beast took refuge on the mountain called Artemisius, and thence passed to the river Ladon
Hercules shot it just as it was about to cross the stream
catching it put it on his shoulders and hastened through Arcadia; heads back; the catching gets no entry (perhaps K⁷, the sought thing caught)
Artemis with Apollo met him, and would have wrested the hind from him, and rebuked him; the seizure is attempted, not carried out; X, perhaps Pr
by pleading necessity and laying the blame on Eurystheus, he appeased the anger of the goddess; X, perhaps Rs
carried the beast alive to Mycenae; the task is done
As a fourth labour he ordered him to bring the Erymanthian boar alive; "now that animal ravaged Psophis" is description, not the reason for the order, so it gets no entry
passing through Pholoe he was entertained by the centaur Pholus
He set roast meat before Hercules, while he himself ate his meat raw

he said he feared to open the jar which belonged to the centaurs in common; a warning, the weakened form of interdiction Propp allows ("a request or bit of advice"); Hercules's asking for wine gets no entry
Hercules, bidding him be of good courage, opened it; the violation, and the centaurs' coming follows from it
scenting the smell, the centaurs arrived at the cave of Pholus, armed with rocks and firs; the attackers arrive; X, perhaps A
The first who dared to enter, Anchius and Agrius, were repelled by Hercules with a shower of brands
the rest of them he shot and pursued as far as Malea; the attackers are routed
Thence they took refuge with Chiron

Hercules shot an arrow at them, which, passing through the arm of Elatus, stuck in the knee of Chiron; accidental wounding, entered as bodily injury in line with the accidental killings; the first villainy in the episode, so still move I; perhaps X
Hercules ran up to him, drew out the shaft, and applied a medicine which Chiron gave him; an attempted cure, which fails ("the hurt proving incurable", next sentence); X, perhaps K
when Hercules returned to Pholoe, he beheld Pholus dead; and he buried him
proceeded to the boar hunt. And when he had chased the boar with shouts from a certain thicket
he drove the exhausted animal into deep snow, trapped it; the capture; X, perhaps K⁷
and brought it to Mycenae; the task set in L2-034 is done
The fifth labour he laid on him was to carry out the dung of the cattle of Augeas in a single day
without revealing the command of Eurystheus, said that he would carry out the dung in one day, if Augeas would give him the tithe of the cattle; X, perhaps η (he hides the command to get the cattle)
Augeas was incredulous, but promised; X, perhaps θ if ev 6 were η
Having taken Augeas's son Phyleus to witness, Hercules made a breach in the foundations of the cattle-yard
diverting the courses of the Alpheus and Peneus, which flowed near each other, he turned them into the yard; the task is done

he would not pay the reward; nay more, he denied that he had promised to pay it; withholds the promised reward, harming the hero; no named form; the first villainy, so move I. The offer to arbitrate gets no entry

Phyleus was called by Hercules and bore witness against his father, affirming that he had agreed to give him a reward; Augeas's denial is exposed; move I breaks here for moves II and III and resumes at ev 17
Eurystheus would not admit this labour either among the ten, alleging that it had been performed for hire; move I (the labours) resumes here; X, as at L2-034 ev 14
The sixth labour he enjoined on him was to chase away the Stymphalian birds
To it countless birds had flocked for refuge, fearing to be preyed upon by the wolves
when Hercules was at a loss how to drive the birds from the wood, Athena gave him brazen castanets
By clashing these on a certain mountain that overhung the lake, he scared the birds; uses the agent; X, perhaps N (scaring is chasing them away)
They could not abide the sound, but fluttered up in a fright
in that way Hercules shot them; the task ends here; the solution could as well be placed at ev 21
The seventh labour he enjoined on him was to bring the Cretan bull
Acusilaus says that this was the bull that ferried across Europa for Zeus; background, the first version given
To attack this bull Hercules came to Crete; sets out on the task
in reply to his request for aid, Minos told him to fight and catch the bull for himself; help is asked for and nothing is given; it could also be read as permission to take the bull
he caught it and brought it to Eurystheus; the catching gets no separate entry
having shown it to him he let it afterwards go free
In a rage Augeas, before the voting took place, ordered both Phyleus and Hercules to pack out of Elis; expulsion; opens move II
Phyleus went to Dulichium and dwelt there
Hercules repaired to Dexamenus at Olenus; the expelled hero goes

He found Dexamenus on the point of betrothing perforce his daughter Mnesimache to the centaur Eurytion; forced marriage, a threat Propp lists (A¹⁶, a dragon demands the tsar's daughter as wife); Hercules's finding gets no entry; opens move III
being called upon by him for help; a call for help
he slew Eurytion when that centaur came to fetch his bride; no fight is narrated either way, so no form
The eighth labour he enjoined on him was to bring the mares of Diomedes the Thracian to Mycenae
Hercules sailed with a band of volunteers
having overpowered the grooms who were in charge of the mangers; fight and outcome in one verb, entered once as the outcome
he drove the mares to the sea; the seizure; X, perhaps K¹
the Bistones in arms came to the rescue; they come after the hero to take back what he took; no Propp form matches, so written bare
he committed the mares to the guardianship of Abderus
the mares killed him by dragging him after them; nothing in the events follows from it (the founding of Abdera is etiology); X, perhaps A¹⁴
Hercules fought against the Bistones
slew Diomedes
compelled the rest to flee
bringing the mares he gave them to Eurystheus
The ninth labour he enjoined on Hercules was to bring the belt of Hippolyte; a task, entered like the other labours; perhaps B², because the text says "Hercules was sent to fetch this belt"

Hercules was sent to fetch this belt because Admete, daughter of Eurystheus, desired to get it; a desire told as the reason for the order; the belt has no stated magic ("in token of her superiority"), so a³, a wondrous object
taking with him a band of volunteer comrades in a single ship he set sail and put in to the island of Paros; move I breaks here for move II (ev 3-7) and resumes at ev 8
he came to Mysia, to the court of Lycus, son of Dascylus, and was entertained by him; move I (the journey for the belt) resumes here
in a battle between him and the king of the Bebryces Hercules sided with Lycus
and slew many, amongst others King Mygdon
he took much land from the Bebryces and gave it to Lycus
he received a visit from Hippolyte, who inquired why he was come, and promised to give him the belt; greeting and questioning; the promise is never carried out and gets no entry (perhaps F)
Hera in the likeness of an Amazon went up and down the multitude saying that the strangers who had arrived were carrying off the queen; a disguise and a false report
the Amazons in arms charged on horseback down on the ship; X, perhaps θ (they fall for the deception) or H (attack)
when Hercules saw them in arms, he suspected treachery, and killing Hippolyte; she is killed as a supposed enemy, with no fight told
stripped her of her belt; the thing sought is taken by force
after fighting the rest; no outcome stated
he sailed away and touched at Troy
two of those in the ship landed and were killed by the sons of Minos; murder; opens move II and breaks off move I
Indignant at this, Hercules killed the sons of Minos on the spot; no fight told; perhaps U
besieged the rest closely
they sent envoys to request that in the room of the murdered men he would take two, whom he pleased; X, perhaps I (surrender) or D⁵ (plea)
he raised the siege, and taking on board the sons of Androgeus, son of Minos, to wit, Alcaeus and Sthenelus; two men replace the two murdered, making good the loss

desiring to put the wantonness of Laomedon to the proof, Apollo and Poseidon assumed the likeness of men and undertook to fortify Pergamum for wages; a test of the hero, as the text says; the disguise gets no separate entry
when they had fortified it
he would not pay them their wages; he fails the test; perhaps A (compare L2-038 ev 10 and L2-045 ev 4, the same kind of act done to the hero, entered as A)
Apollo sent a pestilence; harm; no named form; the first villainy, so move I (it is what Propp calls the retribution after a failed test, F contr., which is not in the rules' alphabet)
and Poseidon a sea monster; sending in the monster; its harm is told in ev 6; X, perhaps A
which, carried up by a flood, snatched away the people of the plain; harm; opens move II

oracles foretold deliverance from these calamities if Laomedon would expose his daughter Hesione to be devoured by the sea monster; X, perhaps A¹⁷ (the demand of the princess for devouring, here voiced by oracles)

he exposed her by fastening her to the rocks near the sea; she is put out to be devoured, the threat Propp lists as A¹⁷; done by the hero himself; Propp says taking a demanded princess to the shore is not B; opens move III

Seeing her exposed, Hercules promised to save her on condition of receiving from Laomedon the mares which Zeus had given in compensation for the rape of Ganymede; decides on counteraction, with a condition (as L2-018 ev 2)
On Laomedon's saying that he would give them; a promise (as L2-018 ev 3)
Hercules killed the monster; no fight told
and saved Hesione; "saved" does not say how, so no variety number (compare "released", L2-018 ev 5)
when Laomedon would not give the stipulated reward; withholds a promised reward, as L2-038 ev 10; the first villainy in the episode, so move I

Hercules put to sea after threatening to make war on Troy; he sails on toward Mycenae with the belt. The threat is not carried out in this episode and gets no entry (perhaps C, or a declaration of war as A¹⁹)
he touched at Aenus, where he was entertained by Poltys
as he was sailing away he shot and killed on the Aenian beach a lewd fellow, Sarpedon; nothing follows from it; X, perhaps U
having come to Thasos and subjugated the Thracians who dwelt in the island, he gave it to the sons of Androgeus to dwell in; conquest; the gift gets no entry
being challenged to wrestle by Polygonus and Telegonus, sons of Proteus; wrestling entered as a fight (H¹) rather than as a contest (H²)
he killed them in the wrestling match
having brought the belt to Mycenae he gave it to Eurystheus; the task set in L2-043 is done
As a tenth labour he was ordered to fetch the kine of Geryon from Erythia
journeying through Europe to fetch the kine of Geryon; sets out; "he destroyed many wild beasts" gets no entry
set foot in Libya, and proceeding to Tartessus
being heated by the Sun on his journey; the future giver's action that the hero answers; the form is unclear (not stated as a test or an attack)
he bent his bow at the god; a gesture actually made, not just threatened, which earns the gift ("in admiration of his hardihood")
who in admiration of his hardihood, gave him a golden goblet
in which he crossed the ocean; travel over water
having reached Erythia he lodged on Mount Abas
the dog, perceiving him, rushed at him
but he smote it with his club; the kill is implied by "killed him also" in the next clause
when the herdsman Eurytion came to the help of the dog, Hercules killed him also
Menoetes, who was there pasturing the kine of Hades, reported to Geryon what had occurred; the one who will fight the hero learns of him
coming up with Hercules beside the river Anthemus, as he was driving away the kine; overtakes the hero, who is driving off the cattle; the driving off gets no entry (perhaps K¹)
joined battle with him
and was shot dead
embarking the kine in the goblet and sailing across to Tartessus, gave back the goblet to the Sun; the way back; giving back the goblet gets no entry
passing through Abderia he came to Liguria
Ialebion and Dercynus, sons of Poseidon, attempted to rob him of the kine, but he killed them; the robbery is attempted, not carried out, and gets no entry (perhaps A)
went on his way through Tyrrhenia; move I breaks here for moves II-IV (ev 26-36) and resumes at ev 37
he conveyed the kine and gave them to Eurystheus; the task is done; move I resumes here
who sacrificed them to Hera

Eurystheus ordered Hercules, as an eleventh labour, to fetch golden apples from the Hesperides; "he did not acknowledge the labour of the cattle of Augeas nor that of the hydra" gets no entry (as L2-034 ev 14)
So journeying he came to the river Echedorus; sets out
Cycnus, son of Ares and Pyrene, challenged him to single combat
Ares championed the cause of Cycnus and marshalled the combat
a thunderbolt was hurled between the two and parted the combatants; the struggle ends with no victory
going on foot through Illyria and hastening to the river Eridanus he came to the nymphs, the daughters of Zeus and Themis
They revealed Nereus to him; they point out who holds the knowledge (as L2-015 ev 13); perhaps G⁴

the hero bound him and did not release him till he had learned from him where were the apples and the Hesperides; he is told the way to the object; the seizure ("seized him while he slept") is a capture beforehand, which Propp (p.41) says is not an independent function, and gets no entry
Being informed, he traversed Libya
Being forced to wrestle with him; wrestling entered as a fight, as at ev 9
Hercules hugged him, lifted him aloft, broke and killed him
After Libya he traversed Egypt

at Rhegium a bull broke away and hastily plunging into the sea swam across to Sicily; a loss that sets off a search (ev 29); not a character's villainy, so entered as lack; no named form; opens move II and breaks off move I
having passed through the neighboring country since called Italy ... came to the plain of Eryx
he mingled the bull with his own herds; takes the hero's bull; opens move III
Hercules entrusted the kine to Hephaestus and hurried away in search of the bull; sets out to search
He found it in the herds of Eryx
the king refused to surrender it unless Hercules should beat him in a wrestling bout; a condition to be met (Propp lists defeating a rival as a task); perhaps H or D⁹
Hercules beat him thrice; the condition is met
killed him in the wrestling; goes beyond the condition; perhaps U
taking the bull drove it with the rest of the herd to the Ionian Sea; the bull is recovered, which also ends the lack of move II; perhaps K⁴ (obtained as a result of the contest)
Hera afflicted the cows with a gadfly, and they dispersed among the skirts of the mountains of Thrace; harm; no named form; opens move IV
Hercules went in pursuit, and having caught some, drove them to the Hellespont; but the remainder were thenceforth wild; the scattered cows are caught, but only some

Having with difficulty collected the cows, Hercules blamed the river Strymon, and whereas it had been navigable before, he made it unnavigable by filling it with rocks; X, perhaps U (the river is punished as the culprit)
So Hercules also was seized and haled to the altars; a hostile figure tries to destroy the hero (D8, like the witch who tries to put the hero in the oven); perhaps A¹⁵ (detention). No agent follows.

he burst his bonds and slew both Busiris and his son Amphidamas; the hero's reaction: he frees himself and vanquishes the adversary; the bursting of the bonds is taken as part of the same reaction. If ev 1 is read as A, then K¹⁰ and I⁵ or U.
traversing Asia he put in to Thermydrae, the harbor of the Lindians; travel only.
having loosed one of the bullocks from the cart of a cowherd, he sacrificed it and feasted; X, perhaps A⁵ (plunder). Nothing follows but the curse and an etiology; no lack is stated.
the cowherd, unable to protect himself, stood on a certain mountain and cursed; leads only to the etiology of cursing at the sacrifice.
passing by Arabia he slew Emathion, son of Tithonus; unmotivated killing with no consequence; X, perhaps I⁵.
journeying through Libya to the outer sea he received the goblet from the Sun; directly transferred; its use is only implied by "having crossed to the opposite mainland" in the next clause.

the eagle, offspring of Echidna and Typhon, that was devouring the liver of Prometheus; act told as the reason for the shooting. A helpless sufferer without a request (Propp's d7 case), who later gives advice (ev 11). Perhaps A⁶ (bodily injury, with Prometheus as victim). The crossing ("having crossed to the opposite mainland") gets no entry: it is not a transfer to the object sought.
he shot on the Caucasus the eagle; a service to the sufferer; perhaps I⁵ if ev 8's first act is A.
he released Prometheus, after choosing for himself the bond of olive; frees a captive. Advice follows (ev 11), so this is the donor-type freeing, not K¹⁰ (Propp p.55).
to Zeus he presented Chiron, who, though immortal, consented to die in his stead; X, perhaps part of E⁴ (the price of the release).

Prometheus had told Hercules not to go himself after the apples but to send Atlas, first relieving him of the burden of the sphere; flashback, told where it stands. Prometheus points out the one through whom the object can be had (like F2, where an old man points out a peasant from whom a steed may be had); perhaps G⁴.

when he was come to Atlas in the land of the Hyperboreans, he took the advice and relieved Atlas; taking the sky from Atlas is a service to him. The arrival is plain walking, so G is not singled out (Propp p.51). The apples are "on Atlas among the Hyperboreans".
when Atlas had received three apples from the Hesperides; the object sought reaches Atlas, not the hero; X, perhaps K (obtained by a helper).

not wishing to support the sphere ... "he said that he would himself carry the apples to Eurystheus, and bade Hercules hold up the sky in his stead"; leaving Hercules under the sky is only intended and is not carried out; X, perhaps η¹ or A.

Hercules promised to do so, but succeeded by craft in putting it on Atlas instead ... "he begged Atlas to hold up the sky till he should" ... "put a pad on his head"; a deceitful persuasion aimed at getting the apples. The promise is feigned, so it gets no θ.
he laid the apples down on the ground and took the sphere from Hercules; the deceived party accepts the proposal.
Hercules picked up the apples; the object is seized by cleverness.
and departed; the return begins.

having brought the apples he gave them to Eurystheus; resolves the eleventh labour ("Eurystheus ordered Hercules, as an eleventh labour, to fetch golden apples from the Hesperides"), which was set before this episode began; perhaps only the end of ↓.
on receiving them, bestowed them on Hercules; X, perhaps w° (reward).
Athena got them and conveyed them back again; a restoration with no consequence.
A twelfth labour imposed on Hercules was to bring Cerberus from Hades; a task of supply. Perhaps a with B² (dispatch); since it is not A or a, no new move is opened.
he went to Eumolpus at Eleusis, wishing to be initiated; X, perhaps D (a preparation). "about to depart" is an intention, so it gets no ↑.
he was cleansed by Eumolpus and then initiated; no use of the initiation is narrated; X, perhaps F.
having come to Taenarum in Laconia, where is the mouth of the descent to Hades, he descended through it; a stationary means of passage (G5, the underground passage).
when the souls saw him, they fled, save Meleager and the Gorgon Medusa
Hercules drew his sword against the Gorgon, as if she were alive; X, perhaps H; there is no adversary.
he learned from Hermes that she was an empty phantom
he found Theseus and Pirithous, him who wooed Persephone in wedlock and was therefore bound fast; the binding is a state told in passing; X, perhaps A¹⁵.
they stretched out their hands as if they should be raised from the dead by his might; prisoners beg for freedom. No gift follows.
Theseus, indeed, he took by the hand and raised up; frees a captive.
when he would have brought up Pirithous, the earth quaked and he let go; negative result, though it is caused by the quake and not by the hero's conduct.
he rolled away also the stone of Ascalaphus; X, perhaps E⁴; nothing follows from it for Hercules.
wishing to provide the souls with blood, he slaughtered one of the kine of Hades; X, perhaps A⁵ (against Hades's herd) or E⁷ (a service to the souls); Menoetes's challenge follows.
Menoetes, son of Ceuthonymus, who tended the king, challenged Hercules to wrestle; a hostile figure engages the hero in combat. No agent follows; perhaps H.
being seized round the middle, had his ribs broken; the hero vanquishes the adversary; perhaps I¹.
he was let off at the request of Persephone; X, perhaps U− (pardon).
Hercules asked Pluto for Cerberus
Pluto ordered him to take the animal provided he mastered him without the use of the weapons which he carried; a condition; X, perhaps M or D¹ (a test), or γ (the ban on weapons, which is kept).

cased in his cuirass and covered by the lion's skin, he flung his arms round the head of the brute; a struggle. Through the victory the hero gets the very object of his quest, so this is H and not D (Propp pp.51-52).
though the dragon in its tail bit him, he never relaxed his grip and pressure till it yielded; victory. The bite gets no entry: it is a wound in the fight (the J¹ form), and nothing follows from it.
So he carried it off; obtained as the result of the victory (perhaps K⁴).
and ascended through Troezen
Demeter turned Ascalaphus into a short-eared owl
after showing Cerberus to Eurystheus; the twelfth labour is resolved.
carried him back to Hades
After his labours Hercules went to Thebes and gave Megara to Iolaus
wishing himself to wed; lack of a bride. This is the episode's first lack, so the events before it belong to move I.

Eurytus, prince of Oechalia, had proposed the hand of his daughter Iole as a prize to him who should vanquish himself and his sons in archery; told as already proposed. A bride-winning contest; perhaps H² (competition).
So he came to Oechalia; the departure is told only through the arrival.
he proved himself better than them at archery
Iphitus, the elder of Eurytus's sons, said that Iole should be given to Hercules
yet he did not get the bride ... "Eurytus and the others refused"; negative result of the wedding. Perhaps A (the prize withheld), but nothing in this episode develops from it as a villainy.
some cattle were stolen from Euboea by Autolycus; a theft; new move.
Eurytus supposed that it was done by Hercules; a false suspicion from which nothing develops.
Iphitus did not believe it and went to Hercules; Iphitus sets out, in effect as seeker of the cattle; perhaps C.
as he came from Pherae after saving the dead Alcestis for Admetus; flashback told in passing; X, perhaps K⁹.
he invited him to seek the kine with him; the hero is asked to go.
Hercules promised to do so and entertained him; he agrees to act. The entertaining gets no entry.
going mad again he threw him from the walls of Tiryns; murder by the hero; new move. Move II breaks off here and is not resumed.
Wishing to be purified of the murder; a desire, realized from within, and so a new move. Perhaps a consequence of move III and not a new lack.
he repaired to Neleus, who was prince of the Pylians
Neleus rejected his request on the score of his friendship with Eurytus; X, perhaps F−. What is refused is purification, not a magical agent.
he went to Amyclae and was purified by Deiphobus, son of Hippolytus; the lack is liquidated as a gift (the KF¹ form).
being afflicted with a dire disease on account of the murder of Iphitus; misfortune with no performer named and no form in Propp's list; new move.
he went to Delphi and inquired how he might be rid of the disease

As the Pythian priestess answered him not by oracles; nothing is given. The plunder ("he was fain to plunder the temple, and, carrying off the tripod, to institute an oracle of his own") is told as intended, so it gets no entry of its own: X, perhaps F⁸ or A⁵.
Apollo fought him; hostile combat, after which the oracle is given (ev 63); perhaps H.
Zeus threw a thunderbolt between them; the fight is broken off undecided; X, perhaps E⁹ with no result.

the remedy for his disease was for him to be sold, and to serve for three years, and to pay compensation for the murder to Eurytus; a task of endurance (compare the seven years in the tin kingdom); perhaps F² (a remedy pointed out) or D¹ (three years' service).
Hermes sold Hercules
he was bought by Omphale
Eurytus did not accept the compensation when it was presented to him; X, perhaps N− for one term of the task.
Hercules served Omphale as a slave; the service is performed.
he seized and bound the Cercopes at Ephesus; no offence of theirs is told.

as for Syleus in Aulis, who compelled passing strangers to dig; told only as the reason for the killing, with no form in Propp's list (perhaps A¹⁵). New move; move V breaks off here. The burning of the vines gets no entry of its own and is taken with ev 70.
Hercules killed him with his daughter Xenodoce, after burning the vines with the roots; perhaps I⁵.
he saw the body of Icarus washed ashore and buried it; a service to the dead, given unasked.
In return Daedalus made a portrait statue of Hercules at Pisa; a return for the service, but nothing is transferred to the hero; X, perhaps F (a reward).
which Hercules mistook at night for living and threw a stone and hit it
After his servitude, being rid of his disease; move V resumes and its misfortune is liquidated.
he mustered an army of noble volunteers and sailed for Ilium with eighteen ships of fifty oars each; no motive is told in this episode. Placed in the resumed move V.
he left the guard of the ships to Oicles and himself with the rest of the champions set out to attack the city
Laomedon marched against the ships with the multitude and slew Oicles in battle; battle.
being repulsed by the troops of Hercules, he was besieged; X, perhaps I¹; the decisive victory is ev 82.
Telamon was the first to breach the wall and enter the city, and after him Hercules
he drew his sword and rushed at him, loath that anybody should be reputed a better man than himself; the attack is begun but not carried out; X, perhaps A.
he said he was building an altar to Hercules the Glorious Victor; X, perhaps η (a ruse that averts the attack).
Hercules thanked him
when he had taken the city and shot down Laomedon and his sons, except Podarces; victory. The killing is taken as part of the victory, since the villain is killed in the battle.
he assigned Laomedon's daughter Hesione as a prize to Telamon and allowed her to take with her whomsoever of the captives she would; X, perhaps w° (a reward to Telamon).
she chose her brother Podarces
Hercules said that he must first be a slave and then be ransomed by her; X, perhaps M (set to Hesione).
she took the veil from her head and gave it as a ransom; X, perhaps N.
When Hercules was sailing from Troy, Hera sent grievous storms; harm of no listed form; new move.
which so vexed Zeus that he hung her from Olympus
Hercules sailed to Cos, and the Coans, thinking he was leading a piratical squadron, endeavored to prevent his approach by a shower of stones; the fight begins. Perhaps A or D⁹.
he forced his way in and took the city by night, and slew the king, Eurypylus
Hercules was wounded in the battle by Chalcedon; told after the victory, and so a flashback within the battle. X, perhaps J¹ (a wound in the fight, though nothing is recognized by it) or A⁶.
Zeus snatched him away, so that he took no harm; X, perhaps Rs¹ (carried off through the air), though there is no pursuit.
having laid waste Cos, he came through Athena's agency to Phlegra; X, perhaps G; Phlegra is not the place of anything sought.
sided with the gods in their victorious war on the giants; X, perhaps H and I; no stake of his own is told.
he collected an Arcadian army, and being joined by volunteers from the first men in Greece he marched against Augeas; the setting out on a campaign whose cause is not told here.
Augeas, hearing of the war that Hercules was levying, appointed Eurytus and Cteatus generals of the Eleans
on the expedition Hercules fell sick; hence he concluded a truce with the Molionides; X, perhaps λ (a difficult situation that the enemy later uses).
being apprized of his illness; the enemy receives information about his victim. It is placed in move VIII with the villainy of the same event, which follows it in the text.
they attacked the army and slew many; the truce is broken; new move. Perhaps H (the war goes on).
Hercules beat a retreat; X, perhaps I−.
Hercules waylaid and killed them at Cleonae; killed without a preliminary fight, from ambush.
marching on Elis took the city
having killed Augeas and his sons; perhaps U.
he restored Phyleus and bestowed on him the kingdom; X, perhaps W³ (for Phyleus) or K.
he marched against Pylus
having taken the city
he slew Periclymenus, the most valiant of the sons of Neleus, who used to change his shape in battle
he slew Neleus and his sons, except Nestor
In the fight he also wounded Hades, who was siding with the Pylians; X, perhaps part of I.
he marched against Lacedaemon; placed in move IX together with the villainy that the same event tells after it.
wishing to punish the sons of Hippocoon; the decision to counteract.
still angrier because they had killed the son of Licymnius; told as a reason, and as a flashback ("the Hippocoontids darted out and despatched him with blows of their cudgels"); new move.
having come to Arcadia he begged Cepheus to join him with his sons, of whom he had twenty; X, perhaps D (a request by the hero) or B.
fearing lest, if he quitted Tegea, the Argives would march against it, Cepheus refused to join the expedition; X, perhaps F−. The Argive attack is only feared.
Hercules had received from Athena a lock of the Gorgon's hair in a bronze jar; flashback: a magical agent directly transferred.

gave it to Sterope, daughter of Cepheus, saying that if an army advanced against the city, she was to hold up the lock of hair thrice from the walls; the agent is passed to Sterope. The ban in "provided she did not look before her, the enemy would be turned to flight" gets no entry: it is never tested.
Cepheus and his sons took the field; X, perhaps F⁹ (characters place themselves at the hero's disposal).
in the battle he and his sons perished, and besides them Iphicles, the brother of Hercules; the battle, with the deaths of allies.
Having killed Hippocoon and his sons and subjugated the city; victory. The killing may be the U sought in L2-047 ev 108.
Hercules restored Tyndareus and entrusted the kingdom to him; X, perhaps W³ (for Tyndareus) or K.
having come to Calydon, Hercules wooed Deianira, daughter of Oeneus; lack of a bride, shown by the wooing.
He wrestled for her hand with Achelous, who assumed the likeness of a bull; a fight with a rival. Perhaps M (Propp's task list has defeating a rival) or D⁹.
Hercules broke off one of his horns
So Hercules married Deianira; a marriage with no throne.
Achelous recovered the horn by giving the horn of Amalthea in its stead
Hercules marched with the Calydonians against the Thesprotians; no cause is told.
having taken the city of Ephyra, of which Phylas was king
he had intercourse with the king's daughter Astyoche, and became the father of Tlepolemus
he sent word to Thespius to keep seven of his sons
he killed with a blow of his knuckles endeavored, son of Architeles, when the lad was pouring water on his hands; an accidental killing that leads to exile; new move.
Seeing that it was an accident, the lad's father pardoned Hercules; a magnanimous pardon (Propp's U neg.).

Hercules wished, in accordance with the law, to suffer the penalty of exile, and resolved to depart to Ceyx at Trachis; a self-chosen exile, carried out in ev 12; perhaps A⁹, suffered by the hero on his own choice.

taking Deianira with him, he came to the river Evenus, at which the centaur Nessus sat and ferried passengers across for hire, alleging that he had received the ferry from the gods for his righteousness; X; Nessus's claim to righteousness is perhaps η (a guise).
Hercules crossed the river by himself
on being asked to pay the fare he entrusted Deianira to Nessus to carry over; X, perhaps θ. It makes the assault possible, but no deception by Nessus is told as an act.
in ferrying her across, attempted to violate her; an assault begun but not completed. The nearest form is A¹⁶, which is Propp's threat of forced matrimony. New move.
She cried out, Hercules heard her; a call for help.
shot Nessus to the heart when he emerged from the river; killed without a fight. Perhaps U; Deianira is freed by it (K⁴), but it is one act.

Nessus called Deianira to him and said that if she would have a love charm to operate on Hercules she should mix the seed he had dropped on the ground with the blood that flowed from the wound inflicted by the barb; a deceitful persuasion, as ev 38 shows.
She did so and kept it by her.
being in lack of food; lack of the means of living; new move.
he unloosed and slaughtered one of the bullocks and feasted; the lack is liquidated by force. Against Thiodamas the same act is perhaps A⁵.
when he came to Ceyx at Trachis he was received by him
conquered the Dryopes; no struggle and no cause are told.
the Lapiths, commanded by Coronus, made war on him in a dispute about the boundaries of the country; war; new move.
being besieged he called in the help of Hercules, offering him a share of the country; a call for help with a promise.
So Hercules came to his help; the decision (C) is implicit and gets no entry.
slew Coronus and others
handed the whole country over to Aegimius free; the misfortune of the siege is undone. The offered share is not taken.

He slew also Laogoras, king of the Dryopes, with his children, as he was banqueting in a precinct of Apollo ... "for the king was a wanton fellow and an ally of the Lapiths"; killed without a fight; perhaps U.
he was challenged to single combat by Cycnus a son of Ares and Pelopia; a hostile figure engages the hero in combat; perhaps H.
closing with him Hercules slew him also; perhaps I¹.
king Amyntor took arms and forbade him to march through; hostile engagement. The forbidding is perhaps γ.
when he would have hindered his passage, Hercules slew him also
he mustered an army to attack Oechalia, wishing to punish Eurytus; the offence is not told in this episode.

Being joined by Arcadians, Melians from Trachis, and Epicnemidian Locrians, he slew Eurytus and his sons and took the city; victory. The allies' joining gets no entry (perhaps F⁹), and the killing is perhaps U.
burying those of his own side who had fallen
he pillaged the city and led Iole captive; an abduction whose consequence is Deianira's fear (ev 36); new move. The pillage gets no entry of its own.
he built an altar of Cenaean Zeus
he sent the herald Lichas to Trachis to fetch fine raiment
From him Deianira learned about Iole; the one who will do the harm receives the information.

she supposed that the spilt blood of Nessus was in truth a love-charm, and with it she smeared the tunic; a magical means applied to the victim without his knowledge. Its motive ("fearing that Hercules might love that damsel more than herself") gets no entry (perhaps a).
So Hercules put it on and proceeded to offer sacrifice

performer: the poison (Nessus's blood, put on by Deianira)
note: no sooner was the tunic warmed than the poison of the hydra began to corrode his skin; bodily injury; new move.
he lifted Lichas by the feet, hurled him down from the headland; X, perhaps U, but Lichas is only the bearer.
tore off the tunic, which clung to his body, so that his flesh was torn away with it; a failed attempt to rid himself of the harm; X, perhaps K−.
he was carried on shipboard to Trachis; a return to his place of residence.
Deianira, on learning what had happened, hanged herself; suicide of the one who did the harm, one of Propp's forms of punishment.
after charging Hyllus his elder son by Deianira, to marry Iole when he came of age
proceeded to Mount Oeta, in the Trachinian territory, and there constructed a pyre, mounted it, and gave orders to kindle it; a dying man requests a service.
When no one would do so, Poeas, passing by to look for his flocks, set a light to it; the service is rendered. The others' refusal gets no entry.
On him Hercules bestowed his bow; a direct transfer, as a reward.
Thereafter he obtained immortality; the dying is undone; perhaps T. The ascent in the cloud is told only as "it is said" and is not a census event.
being reconciled to Hera; X, perhaps U− (pardon).
he married her daughter Hebe
his sons fled from Eurystheus and came to Ceyx; a flight whose cause is not told as an act.
Eurystheus demanded their surrender and threatened war; the villain demands his victims. Perhaps Pr² (the pursuer demands the guilty); the war is only threatened.
quitting Trachis, fled through Greece; departure as flight.
Being pursued, they came to Athens, and sitting down on the altar of Mercy, claimed protection; pursuit. The claim of protection gets no entry of its own and leads to the rescue in ev 5.
Refusing to surrender them; protectors refuse the pursuer's demand and take on the fight, like the blacksmiths of Rs5.
the Athenians bore the brunt of war with Eurystheus
slew his sons, Alexander, Iphimedon, Eurybius, Mentor and Perimedes
Eurystheus himself fled in a chariot, but was pursued; pursuit, here by the hero's side.
and slain by Hyllus just as he was driving past the Scironian cliffs; perhaps U.
Hyllus cut off his head and gave it to Alcmena; X, perhaps part of U.
she gouged out his eyes with weaving-pins; punishment done on the dead villain.
the Heraclids came to attack Peloponnese; the text calls this "their return" ("a year had elapsed from their return").
and they captured all the cities
a plague visited the whole of Peloponnese; harm with no performer named; new move.
an oracle declared that this happened on account of the Heraclids, because they had returned before the proper time; the misfortune is made known, and it causes their departure.
they quitted Peloponnese and retired to Marathon and dwelt there; no end of the plague is told.
sought to effect the return of the Heraclids; a desire to return. The inquiry ("So he went to Delphi and inquired how they should return") gets no entry of its own.
the god said that they should await the third crop before returning; an interdiction on returning early; perhaps F² (an instruction).
Hyllus supposed that the third crop signified three years; and having waited that time he returned with his army; the return breaks the interdiction unwittingly, as ev 8 shows; perhaps ↑.
in another battle the Peloponnesians were victorious, and Aristomachus was slain; the hero's side loses the fight.
they inquired of the oracle concerning their return; X; perhaps a renewed a.
the god having given the same answer as before; X, perhaps γ repeated.
Temenus blamed him, saying that when they had obeyed the oracle they had been unfortunate

not a crop of the earth, but a crop of a generation ... "by the narrows he meant the broad-bellied sea on the right of the Isthmus"; the route is shown, and ships are built in response (ev 9); perhaps F².
Temenus made ready the army and built ships in Locris; X, perhaps ↑.
Aristodemus was killed by a thunderbolt; X, perhaps A; nothing follows from it.
there appeared to them a soothsayer reciting oracles in a fine frenzy, whom they took for a magician sent by the Peloponnesians to be the ruin of the army; a mistaken belief.
Hippotes, son of Phylas, son of Antiochus, son of Hercules, threw a javelin at him, and hit and killed him; a murder by a Heraclid, which brings the calamity. New move; move I breaks off here.
In consequence of that, the naval force perished with the destruction of the fleet; harm to the heroes; new move. Move II breaks off here.
the land force suffered from famine; the same calamity; X, perhaps a further A.
the army disbanded; the consequence of the calamity.

the god said that these things were done by the soothsayer and he ordered him to banish the slayer for ten years and to take for his guide the Three-Eyed One; the misfortune is explained and orders are given. One act, so one entry.
So they banished Hippotes; the slayer of move II is punished, so move II resumes here.
sought for the Three-Eyed One; they set out on a search; perhaps C.
they chanced to light on Oxylus, son of Andraemon, a man sitting on a one-eyed horse; the helper is found by chance.
guessing the purport of the oracle, they made him their guide; the leading is implied, not told.
having engaged the enemy
they got the better of him both by land and sea, and slew Tisamenus
Their allies, Pamphylus and Dymas, the sons of Aegimius, also fell in the fight

When they had made themselves masters of Peloponnese, they set up three altars of Paternal Zeus, and sacrificed upon them; the lack of move I (the return) is liquidated, so move I resumes here. The altars and sacrifice get no entry.
cast lots for the cities
they brought a pitcher of water, and resolved that each should cast in a lot
Cresphontes, wishing to have Messene allotted to him; a desire; new move.
threw in a clod of earth; deception by other means.
As the clod was dissolved in the water, it could not be but that the other two lots should turn up ... "Cresphontes got Messene"; obtained by cleverness.
on the altars on which they sacrificed they found signs lying
the seers said; interpretation only.
Zeus loved her; a desire for a bride.
turning himself into a tame bull; a disguise, which Propp gives as the first step of trickery; the persuasion itself is not told.
he mounted her on his back; the object sought is seized by cunning. The same act is the A¹ of L3-002.
conveyed her through the sea to Crete; X, perhaps G² or ↓.
There Zeus bedded with her; X, perhaps W² (a union, not a marriage).
On the disappearance of Europa; the abduction told in L3-001, given here as the reason for the dispatch. Hero: Cadmus.
her father Agenor sent out his sons in search of her, telling them not to return until they had found Europa; direct dispatch, with a threat.
went forth in search of her
after diligent search, they could not find Europa; the misfortune is not liquidated.
they gave up the thought of returning home; X, perhaps ↓−, held back by the dispatcher's condition.
Phoenix settled in Phoenicia
Cilix settled near Phoenicia, and all the country subject to himself near the river Pyramus he called Cilicia; X, perhaps W³.
Cadmus and Telephassa took up their abode in Thrace; the hero's settlement.
