Cadmus and Telephassa took up their abode in Thrace
Thasus founded a city Thasus in an island off Thrace and dwelt there
Asterius, prince of the Cretans, married Europa and brought up her children
they loved a boy called Miletus; the lack of a beloved (Propp's a1 includes a friend). Told in the text as the reason for the quarrel.
they quarrelled with each other; X, perhaps H.
As the boy was more friendly to Sarpedon, Minos went to war; war on the hero; new move.
and had the better of it; the hero's side loses.
and the others fled; departure as flight.
Miletus landed in Caria and there founded a city
Sarpedon allied himself with Cilix, who was at war with the Lycians, and having stipulated for a share of the country; X, perhaps E (a service for a reward). No fighting is told.
he became king of Lycia; accession to the throne only.
Zeus granted him to live for three generations; X, perhaps F¹ (a quality given, never used) or w°.
Minos, residing in Crete, passed laws
Asterius dying childless; the death of an elder, which leaves the throne open.
Minos wished to reign over Crete; a desire for the kingdom.
his claim was opposed; X, perhaps A.
he alleged that he had received the kingdom from the gods; X, perhaps L; the text does not say the claim is false.
in proof of it he said that whatever he prayed for would be done
in sacrificing to Poseidon he prayed that a bull might appear from the depths; a service of a religious kind (Propp puts prayer under E7). No D precedes it.
promising to sacrifice it when it appeared; X, perhaps γ, since this undertaking is later broken.
Poseidon did send him up a fine bull; the agent by which the claim is proved.
Minos obtained the kingdom; the lack is liquidated; perhaps W³.
he sent the bull to the herds; the broken promise. Poseidon's anger follows from it (ev 14).
and sacrificed another
he extended his rule over almost all the islands
angry at him for not sacrificing the bull, Poseidon made the animal savage; new move; perhaps A¹¹ (a spell cast on something).
contrived that Pasiphae should conceive a passion for it; a spell cast on a person. Perhaps a, since what follows is the pursuit of the desire and not a breaking of the spell.
In her love for the bull she found an accomplice in Daedalus; a helper is acquired (F⁹ or F⁵).
who had been banished from Athens for murder; a flashback told in passing.
He constructed a wooden cow on wheels, took it, hollowed it out in the inside, sewed it up in the hide of a cow which he had skinned; the agent is prepared.
set it in the meadow in which the bull used to graze; X, perhaps G.
Then he introduced Pasiphae into it; the hero is delivered, inside the agent, to where the object of her desire is. Perhaps η (a disguise).
the bull came and coupled with it, as if it were a real cow; her desire is fulfilled. Perhaps θ (the bull deceived). It does not answer ev 1 as the breaking of a spell.
she gave birth to Asterius, who was called the Minotaur
Catreus hid the oracles, but Althaemenes heard of them; a misfortune (foretold: "he would die by the hand of one of his children") is made known and causes the departure. No A or a is told.
fearing to be his father's murderer; a motive.
he set out from Crete with his sister Apemosyne
put in at a place in Rhodes
having taken possession of it he called it Cretinia; X, perhaps W³.
having ascended the mountain called Atabyrium
he beheld the islands round about; and descrying Crete also
calling to mind the gods of his fathers he founded an altar of Atabyrian Zeus; X, perhaps E⁷ (a religious service), from which nothing follows.
Hermes loved her; the desire is the god's.
she fled from him; her flight implies his pursuit, which ev 3 confirms.
he could not catch her, because she excelled him in speed of foot; saved by swift flight.
he spread fresh hides on the path; deception by other means (like the knives set at the window).
returning from the spring, she slipped; she reacts mechanically to the device.
and so was deflowered; the harm, of no listed form; new move. For Hermes it is also the end of his lack (K).
She revealed to her brother what had happened; the misfortune is made known. It is followed by no counteraction.
deeming the god a mere pretext, kicked her to death; murder; new move. Perhaps U, as he takes it.
Catreus gave Aerope and Clymene to Nauplius to sell into foreign lands; expulsion, by the hero. Nothing further follows from it in this episode.
in the grip of old age Catreus yearned to transmit the kingdom to his son Althaemenes; a desire; new move.
went for that purpose to Rhodes
having landed from the ship with the heroes at a desert place of the island; an arrival in another country, where he is not recognized (ev 5).
he was chased by the cowherds, who imagined that they were pirates on a raid
He told them the truth; X, perhaps Q (an attempt at recognition that fails).
they could not hear him for the barking of the dogs
while they pelted him; the pursuers try to kill him.
Althaemenes arrived
killed him with the cast of a javelin, not knowing him to be Catreus; murder; new move.
in chasing a mouse
fell into a jar of honey; X, perhaps θ (the hero's own mishap).
and was drowned; a death by accident with no performer. A¹⁴ is Propp's murder, and it is answered by revival (ev 17).
On his disappearance Minos made a great search; counteraction; perhaps ↑.
consulted diviners as to how he should find him; X, perhaps B¹ (a call for help).
the man who could best describe that cow's color would also restore his son to him alive; a riddle-like ordeal.
Polyidus, son of Coeranus, compared the color of the cow to the fruit of the bramble; the task is solved.
being compelled to seek for the child; dispatch by command.
he found him by means of a sort of divination; led to where the object of search is. Perhaps K, but the child is found dead.
Minos declaring that he must recover him alive; a task.
he was shut up with the dead body; the task is enforced; X, perhaps A¹⁵.
he saw a serpent going towards the corpse
He threw a stone and killed it, fearing to be killed himself if any harm befell the body; X, perhaps I⁵ or E. It leads to the showing of the herb.
another serpent came, and, seeing the former one dead, departed
returned, bringing a herb, and placed it on the whole body of the other; the agent appears and is shown, unintentionally (perhaps F² or F⁶).
the dead serpent came to life; it shows what the agent does; X, perhaps K⁹ for the serpent.
Polyidus applied the same herb to the body of Glaucus; the agent is used; X, perhaps N.
raised him from the dead; a slain person is revived. This also solves the task of ev 9 (N), but it is one act.
Minos had now got back his son; a restatement of ev 17.
he did not suffer Polyidus to depart to Argos until he had taught Glaucus the art of divination; detention; new move. Perhaps M (a task).
Polyidus taught him on compulsion; a capacity directly given to the hero (Propp's fourth class of agents).
when he was sailing away he bade Glaucus spit into his mouth; a persuasion that hides its purpose.
Glaucus did so
forgot the art of divination; the magical capacity is taken away; new move.
When Telephassa died, Cadmus buried her; X, perhaps β² (death of a parent, p.26); no harm is prepared by it in this text, and the burial is no function.
after being hospitably received by the Thracians; X, perhaps D² (greeting), but no test follows and nothing is given.
he came to Delphi to inquire about Europa; X, perhaps a¹ (the lack of Europa, created in an earlier episode, restated here only as the purpose of the inquiry) or D (approach to a consultant).

The god told him not to trouble about Europa, but to be guided by a cow, and to found a city wherever she should fall down for weariness; an order addressed to the hero (inverted interdiction, p.27); perhaps B² (dispatch by command), but no misfortune or lack is made known.
After receiving such an oracle he journeyed through Phocis; X, perhaps ↑.

falling in with a cow among the herds of Pelagon, he followed it behind; the order of ev 4 fulfilled (a fulfilled order corresponds to a violated interdiction, p.27); perhaps G³ (he is led); the chance finding of the cow (perhaps F⁵) is given no entry of its own.
after traversing Boeotia, it sank down where is now the city of Thebes; X, perhaps G (arrival at the place sought).

Wishing to sacrifice the cow to Athena, he sent some of his companions to draw water from the spring of Ares; X, perhaps γ² (an order whose fulfilment exposes those sent to harm), but it is addressed to the companions, not to the hero.

a dragon ... guarded the spring and destroyed most of those that were sent; murder of the hero's companions; "which some said was the offspring of Ares" is a report of authorities and is not transcribed.
In his indignation Cadmus killed the dragon; the villain killed; no fight narrated, so no H and no variety number (perhaps I⁵, killed without a preliminary fight); perhaps U.
by the advice of Athena sowed its teeth; X, perhaps F² (agent pointed out) or F³ (agent prepared); what grows from the teeth gives the hero no help in this text.
there rose from the ground armed men whom they called Sparti; X, perhaps F⁶ (agents sprouting out of the ground, p.45), but they serve the hero in nothing.
These slew each other, some in a chance brawl, and some in ignorance; X; Pherecydes's version is a report of an authority and is not transcribed.
five of them survived; X.

Cadmus, to atone for the slaughter, served Ares for an eternal year; a term of service (a form of test, p.39-40, service for three years) completed and followed by reward (ev 16); no D narrated; perhaps X (penance) or U.
After his servitude Athena procured for him the kingdom; accession to the throne only (Propp's third form of W); bare W because Propp's forms of W carry no numbers.
Zeus gave him to wife Harmonia; marriage (Propp's second form of W); bare W as at ev 16.
all the gods quitted the sky, and feasting in the Cadmea celebrated the marriage with hymns; X, part of the wedding already entered.

Cadmus gave her a robe and the necklace wrought by Hephaestus; X, perhaps F¹, but given by the hero and not used in this episode; the "some say" and Pherecydes on the necklace's origin are not transcribed.
Zeus loved Semele; desire for a woman (lack of a bride or of a human being generally, a¹, p.35); perhaps X.
and bedded with her unknown to Hera; the desire of ev 1 satisfied; no variety number; perhaps X.
Zeus had agreed to do for her whatever she asked; X (told as prior, a flashback); perhaps λ (an agreement later turned to harm), but it is not a deceitful agreement made by the villain.
deceived by Hera; trickery by the villain; the form of the deceit is not told, so no variety number.
she asked that he would come to her as he came when he was wooing Hera; the victim acts on the deceit and unwittingly brings on her own harm; no variety number.
Unable to refuse, Zeus came to her bridal chamber in a chariot, with lightnings and thunderings; X, perhaps θ (Zeus too is bound into the deceit by his agreement).
and launched a thunderbolt; X; the villainy is entered at ev 7, where the harm is done; perhaps it belongs here, as the act that causes the death.
But Semele expired of fright; the death Hera's deceit contrived; performer uncertain (Hera contrives it, Zeus's thunder is the means, the text says she died "of fright").
Zeus, snatching the sixth-month abortive child from the fire; X, perhaps Rs or K (part of the misfortune averted).
sewed it in his thigh; X.
the other daughters of Cadmus spread a report that Semele had bedded with a mortal man, and had falsely accused Zeus; X, perhaps A (slander) or L; nothing follows from it in this episode.
at the proper time Zeus undid the stitches and gave birth to Dionysus; X, perhaps K (the child saved from the misfortune).
and entrusted him to Hermes; X.
he conveyed him to Ino and Athamas; X.
and persuaded them to rear him as a girl; X, perhaps γ² (a suggestion whose fulfilment brings Hera's anger) or D⁷ (a request).
But Hera indignantly drove them mad; harm by maddening; no variety number (perhaps A¹¹, a spell).

Athamas hunted his elder son Learchus as a deer and killed him; murder of a member of the family; a new villainy and so a new move by the rule, though it is the working-out of the madness of ev 3 (compare Propp's combined forms, p.33).
Ino threw Melicertes into a boiling cauldron; murder; a new villainy, with the same doubt as ev 4.
then carrying it with the dead child she sprang into the deep; X, perhaps U (self-destruction); the sailors' names and the Isthmian games that follow are etiology and are not transcribed.
Dionysus discovered the vine; X, perhaps F⁵ (agent found), but the vine is not used as an agent in this episode.
being driven mad by Hera; harm by maddening; no variety number (perhaps A¹¹).
he roamed about Egypt and Syria; the victim's journey without search that follows the harm (p.39); perhaps X.
At first he was received by Proteus, king of Egypt; X, perhaps D² (greeting), but no test and no gift.
afterwards he arrived at Cybela in Phrygia; X, perhaps G.
after he had been purified by Rhea; the madness of ev 2 is not mentioned again, so the purification is taken as its liquidation; no variety number (perhaps K⁸, spell broken); perhaps X.
and learned the rites of initiation; X, perhaps F (a capacity given), but no use of it as an agent is narrated.
he received from her the costume; X, perhaps F¹ (agent directly transferred), but the costume has no power or use in this text.
and hastened through Thrace against the Indians; departure on an expedition; perhaps X.
he was the first who insulted; X, perhaps A (the insult), but no harm is done by it; the expulsion is entered at ev 11.
and expelled him; expulsion.
Dionysus took refuge in the sea with Thetis, daughter of Nereus; X, perhaps Rs⁴ (the hero hides), but no pursuit is narrated.
the Bacchanals were taken prisoners together with the multitude of Satyrs that attended him; imprisonment of the hero's company; performer not named (passive).
afterwards the Bacchanals were suddenly released; the captives freed; the agent is not named.

and Dionysus drove Lycurgus mad; punishment of the one who insulted, expelled and imprisoned; it answers the villainies of moves II and III, and is written in III, the move then under way; perhaps A (a harm by the hero, judged by what follows, ev 16).

in his madness he struck his son Dryas dead with an axe, imagining that he was lopping a branch of a vine; X, perhaps A¹⁴; taken as the working of the punishment of ev 15; nothing is said to follow from the killing itself.
when he had cut off his son's extremities, he recovered his senses; X.
But the land remaining barren; a lack (of fruit, the means of existence; perhaps a⁵); no agent named, so not A.
the god declared oracularly that it would bear fruit if Lycurgus were put to death; the remedy made known and the deed demanded, which sends the Edonians to act; no variety number; perhaps X.
On hearing that, the Edonians led him to Mount Pangaeum and bound him; X, perhaps U (the punishment begun).
there by the will of Dionysus he died, destroyed by horses; punishment of Lycurgus; the land's recovery (K) is not narrated.
Having traversed Thrace and the whole of India; X, perhaps ↑.
and set up pillars there; X.
he came to Thebes; X, perhaps o (the Thebans are later shown he is a god, ev 29), but the text does not say he came unrecognized.
forced the women to abandon their houses and rave in Bacchic frenzy on Cithaeron; a harm by the hero, no reason given; no variety number (perhaps A¹¹ or A⁹).
he attempted to put a stop to these proceedings; X, perhaps C (counteraction) by Pentheus; an attempt, not carried through.
coming to Cithaeron to spy on the Bacchanals; reconnaissance by the hero's opponent; no variety number; perhaps X.

he was torn limb from limb by his mother Agave in a fit of madness; for she thought he was a wild beast; the opponent's death, which ends the Theban events and shows Dionysus a god (ev 29), taken as punishment; perhaps A¹⁴.
having shown the Thebans that he was a god; recognition of the hero; the coming to Argos in the same event is no function; perhaps X.

because they did not honor him, he drove the women mad; punishment for the dishonour; the not honouring, told as the reason, is given no entry (perhaps A, or δ of an unstated interdiction); perhaps A.
they on the mountains devoured the flesh of the infants whom they carried at their breasts; X, perhaps A¹⁴; the working of the punishment of ev 30; nothing follows from it.
wishing to be ferried across from Icaria to Naxos he hired a pirate ship of Tyrrhenians; X, perhaps a (a wish) or F⁴ (a vessel purchased).
when they had put him on board; X, perhaps η or θ, but no deceit is narrated.
they sailed past Naxos and made for Asia, intending to sell him; abduction of the hero; the intended sale is not carried out.
he turned the mast and oars into snakes; X, perhaps H or I (the hero's magic turned against the abductors).
and filled the vessel with ivy and the sound of flutes; X.
And the pirates went mad; X, perhaps U (punishment begun) or I.
and leaped into the sea; X, perhaps I or K (the abductors gone, the hero free), but neither defeat nor freeing is narrated as such.
and were turned into dolphins; punishment of the abductors by transformation; no fight or pursuit precedes (p.63).
Thus men perceived that he was a god and honored him; recognition of the hero; perhaps X.
having brought up his mother from Hades and named her Thyone; a dead person brought back (perhaps K⁹, revival); the death was narrated in another episode (L3-019), not in this one.
he ascended up with her to heaven; X, perhaps T (transfiguration) or W.
Cadmus and Harmonia quitted Thebes and went to the Encheleans; the hero leaves home; no reason is given and no harm precedes it; perhaps X.
the Encheleans were being attacked by the Illyrians; war made on the hero's hosts.

the god declared by an oracle that they would get the better of the Illyrians if they had Cadmus and Harmonia as their leaders; X, perhaps B (the means made known); the call to the hero is entered at ev 4.

They believed him, and made them their leaders against the Illyrians; the hero is called to meet the misfortune; no variety number (perhaps B¹, call for help); the hero's own agreement (C) is not narrated.
and got the better of them; victory over the attackers; no fight described, so no H and no variety number.
And Cadmus reigned over the Illyrians; accession to a throne only (Propp's third form of W), bare W; the birth of Illyrius is genealogy.
he was, along with Harmonia, turned into a serpent; X, perhaps T (a new appearance), but not as Propp's forms of T give it.
and sent away by Zeus to the Elysian Fields; X.

the government was usurped by Lycus, brother of Nycteus, so long as Laius was a child; seizure of the child king's throne (plunder in other forms, A⁵); perhaps W (the hero gains power), since no harm to Laius follows in this episode.
they had killed Phlegyas, son of Ares and Dotis the Boeotian; flashback, told as the reason for the flight; murder; a new move by the rule.
Both of them had fled [ from Euboea]; flashback; departure in the form of flight (p.39); perhaps X.
they took up their abode at Hyria; flashback; X.
thence having come to Thebes; flashback; X.
they were enrolled as citizens through their friendship with Pentheus; flashback ends here; X.

after being chosen commander-in-chief by the Thebans, Lycus compassed the supreme power; X; the same usurpation already entered at ev 1, told again after the flashback; the narrative returns here to the time of move I, but the rule keeps it in move II; perhaps A⁵ or W.
and reigned for twenty years; X, perhaps W; his murder by Zethus and Amphion, announced here, is narrated in L3-031.
Zeus had intercourse with her; X, perhaps A (seduction), but nothing harmful is said of it.
When she was with child, and her father threatened her; a threat, not carried out, and not a form Propp lists; X, perhaps A.
she ran away to Epopeus at Sicyon; departure as flight (p.39); perhaps X, as no villainy precedes it.
and was married to him; marriage (Propp's second form of W), bare W.
In a fit of despondency Nycteus killed himself; X.
after charging Lycus to punish Epopeus and Antiope; X, perhaps A¹³ (an order to harm the hero) or B² (a dispatch by command, with Lycus as the one sent).
Lycus marched against Sicyon, subdued it; war on the hero's new home.
slew Epopeus; murder of the hero's husband; a new villainy and so a new move by the rule, though Propp would combine forms done at once (p.33).
and led Antiope away captive; abduction of the hero; new move, with the same doubt as ev 8.
On the way she gave birth to two sons at Eleurethae in Boeotia; X.
The infants were exposed; exposure of the hero; performer not named (passive); no variety number (nearest A⁹, expulsion, or A¹⁰).
but a neatherd found and reared them; X, perhaps Rs or K (the exposed children saved).
he called the one Zethus and the other Amphion; X.
Zethus paid attention to cattle-breeding; X.
but Amphion practised minstrelsy; X.
for Hermes had given him a lyre; flashback; the lyre is directly given and is later used to wondrous effect (ev 14).
Lycus and his wife Dirce imprisoned Antiope and treated her despitefully; imprisonment of the hero's mother.
one day her bonds were loosed of themselves; the captive freed.

unknown to her keepers she came to her sons cottage, begging that they would take her in; the one wronged comes to the hero with a request, which brings the hero into the action; no variety number; perhaps o (arrival unrecognized), but Antiope is not the hero.
They recognized their mother; recognition of parent and children after separation (p.62).
and slew Lycus; the villain killed after the misfortune is already undone, taken as punishment; perhaps I (killed without a fight).
but Dirce they tied to a bull; punishment of the villain ("tied to the tail of a horse", p.63).
and flung her dead body into the spring that is called Dirce after her; X; the naming is etiology.

having succeeded to the sovereignty they fortified the city, the stones following Amphion's lyre; accession to the throne (Propp's third form of W), bare W; the fortifying with the lyre, the use of the agent of ev 6, is given no entry (perhaps T², a marvellous building).
and they expelled Laius; expulsion, a harm by the hero; its sequel (Laius in the Peloponnese) lies outside this episode.
Niobe said that she was more blessed with children than Latona; X, perhaps δ (a transgression without a stated interdiction, p.27).
Stung by the taunt, Latona incited Artemis and Apollo against them; the villainy ordered; no variety number, since the text says "incited", not "ordered to kill" (perhaps A¹³).
Artemis shot down the females in the house; murder; the carrying-out of ev 2, but a new villainy by the rule, so a new move.
Apollo killed all the males together as they were hunting on Cithaeron; murder; a new move, with the same doubt as ev 3.
Of the males Amphion alone was saved, and of the females Chloris the elder; X; the marriage of Chloris is genealogy and Telesilla's version is a report of an authority.
Niobe herself quitted Thebes and went to her father Tantalus at Sipylus; the hero leaves home after the misfortune; perhaps X.
on praying to Zeus; X, perhaps E⁷ (a prayer, p.43), but no donor acts first.
she was transformed into a stone; X, perhaps T or F (the prayer answered); the flowing tears are description.
he pierced the child's ankles with brooches; bodily injury; the oracle to Laius and his begetting the child come before the census's first event and are not transcribed.
and gave it to a herdsman to expose; exposure ordered; a new villainy by the rule, though done at once with ev 1; no variety number (perhaps A¹³, the ordering of a death).
But the herdsman exposed it on Cithaeron; the exposure carried out; a harmful act by a figure told of in passing, so a new villainy and a new move by the rule; no variety number (nearest A⁹ or A¹⁰).
the neatherds of Polybus, king of Corinth, found the infant and brought it to his wife Periboea; X, perhaps Rs or K (the exposed child saved).
She adopted him and passed him off as her own; X.
after she had healed his ankles she called him Oedipus; the injury of ev 1 healed; move I, broken off after ev 1 by moves II and III, resumes here; no variety number; the naming is no function.
When the boy grew up and excelled his fellows in strength; X; back in move III after the resumption of move I at ev 6.
they spitefully twitted him with being supposititious; X, perhaps A (an insult), though what follows is his search to know his parents.
He inquired of Periboea, but could learn nothing; a lack realized from within, knowledge of his parentage, which provokes the quest to Delphi; no variety number (perhaps a⁶, other forms); perhaps X.
so he went to Delphi and inquired about his true parents; X, perhaps ↑ (departure on a quest); the departure is entered at ev 12.
The god told him not to go to his native land, because he would murder his father and lie with his mother; interdiction.
believing himself to be the son of his nominal parents, he left Corinth; the hero leaves home; perhaps X.
riding in a chariot through Phocis he fell in with Laius driving in a chariot in a certain narrow road; X.
Polyphontes, the herald of Laius, ordered him to make way; an order addressed to the hero (inverted interdiction); perhaps X, as it comes from a hostile stranger, not from a protector.
because he disobeyed and delayed; the order of ev 14 broken; told as the reason for the harm that follows in the same event.
and killed one of his horses; harm to the hero's property; no variety number (perhaps A⁵).

Oedipus in a rage killed both Polyphontes and Laius; the attackers killed; no fight narrated, so no H and no variety number; perhaps A¹⁴ (the killing of his father, whose consequences come in another episode) or U.
and arrived in Thebes; he enters his native land, against the interdiction of ev 11; perhaps o (arrival home unrecognized), but the text does not say he came unrecognized.

In his reign a heavy calamity befell Thebes. For Hera sent the Sphinx; X, perhaps A (the calamity) or B² (the Sphinx, who is the hero, dispatched); taken as the arrival of the one who harms (an arrival is not a function, p.27-28); the harm itself is entered at ev 5; the Sphinx's parentage and form are description.
having learned a riddle from the Muses; X, perhaps F¹ (a thing given, later the means of her hold on Thebes), but the riddle is no magical agent.
she sat on Mount Phicium, and propounded it to the Thebans; a riddle to be guessed, a difficult task (p.60).

the Thebans were in possession of an oracle which declared that they should be rid of the Sphinx whenever they had read her riddle; so they often met and discussed the answer; X, perhaps C (counteraction decided).
when they could not find it; the task not solved, told as the reason for what follows; minus as for Propp's negative results (p.117, note 4); perhaps X.

the Sphinx used to snatch away one of them and gobble him up; the first harm narrated in the episode, so move I's villainy; no variety number (nearest A¹⁷, cannibalism, which Propp lists as a threat, or A¹⁴).
When many had perished, and last of all Creon's son Haemon; X, the villainy of ev 5 repeated.
Creon made proclamation that to him who should read the riddle he would give both the kingdom and the wife of Laius; a call for help from the king, with promises (p.37).
On hearing that, Oedipus found the solution, declaring that the riddle of the Sphinx referred to man; the task solved.
So the Sphinx threw herself from the citadel; the one who harmed takes her own life (suicide is among Propp's forms of punishment, p.63), though she is the census's hero; perhaps I.
Oedipus both succeeded to the kingdom; accession to the throne, as promised at L3-038 ev 7 (Propp's third form of W), bare W.

and unwittingly married his mother; marriage (Propp's second form of W), bare W; the marriage is later the ground of disaster, so perhaps δ of the oracle of L3-036 ev 11; the children are genealogy and Eurygania is a "some say".
When the secret afterwards came to light; the deeds are exposed, and what follows (death, blinding, expulsion) is ruin for the one exposed; perhaps Q (recognition of parent and child).
Jocasta hanged herself in a noose; X, perhaps U.
after he had put out his eyes; X, perhaps U (self-punishment) or A⁶ (bodily injury).

and cursed his sons, who saw him cast out of the city without lifting a hand to help him; X, perhaps A¹¹ (a curse as a spell), but no effect of the curse is narrated; the sons' failure to help is no function.
Oedipus was driven from Thebes; expulsion of the hero; the first villainy, so still move I; perhaps U (banishment after exposure).
having come with Antigone to Colonus in Attica; X, perhaps ↑ or G.
he sat down there as a suppliant; X.
was kindly received by Theseus; X, perhaps K (banishment has no specific liquidation, p.111) or D².
and died not long afterwards; X.
Eteocles and Polynices made a compact with each other concerning the kingdom and resolved that each should rule alternately for a year at a time; X.
Polynices was the first to rule; X (the first of the two versions, which the census takes).
after a year he handed over the kingdom to Eteocles; X.
So, being banished from Thebes; expulsion of the hero; performer not named.
Polynices came to Argos, taking with him the necklace and the robe; the banished hero's departure (p.111, banishment motivating departure); perhaps X; he already holds the necklace and robe, so no F.
Polynices went up to his palace by night; X.

and engaged in a fight with Tydeus; a brawl at night with a stranger, which ends in a bride, an ally and a promise of help (ev 11-14), not in the object of the hero's quest (p.51-52); perhaps H; the outcome (E) is not narrated.
who had fled from Calydon; flashback, told in passing; X.
At the sudden outcry Adrastus appeared and parted them; X, perhaps the undecided end of the fight of ev 7.
remembering the words of a certain seer who told him to yoke his daughters in marriage to a boar and a lion; X; the seer's words are a flashback.

he accepted them both as bridegrooms, because they had on their shields, the one the forepart of a boar, and the other the forepart of a lion; X, perhaps Q (recognized by a mark) or a betrothal; the weddings are entered at ev 12-13.
Tydeus married Deipyle; a marriage (Propp's second form of W), bare W, performed by a figure other than the census's hero.
Polynices married Argia; marriage (Propp's second form of W), bare W.

Adrastus promised that he would restore them both to their native lands; a promise of service (Propp counts a helper's bare promise as F⁹, p.45); perhaps X (an act only intended); the mustering that follows lies outside the census's events.
being a seer and foreseeing that all who joined in the expedition except Adrastus were destined to perish; X.
shrank from it himself; X.
and discouraged the rest; X, perhaps γ (an interdiction, but not one whose breach harms the one who gave it).

Polynices went to Iphis, son of Alector, and begged to know how Amphiaraus could be compelled to go to the war; reconnaissance about the victim, through a third person; no variety number (perhaps ε³).
He answered that it could be done if Eriphyle got the necklace; the one seeking receives the information.
Amphiaraus had forbidden Eriphyle to accept gifts from Polynices; interdiction (told as prior, a flashback).
Polynices gave her the necklace and begged her to persuade Amphiaraus to go to the war; persuasion by a gift to be accepted (p.29, "a witch tries to have a ring accepted").

he had made it up with him and sworn to let Eriphyle decide any future dispute he might have with Adrastus; flashback, told in passing; X, perhaps λ (the agreement that compels assent, p.30), but it was not made by deceit.
Eriphyle accepted the necklace; the interdiction of ev 6 broken; perhaps θ (acceptance of the persuasion of ev 7), but she is not deceived.
and persuaded him to march with Adrastus; the victim demanded and sent to his fate, through the binding agreement of ev 8 (p.32-33).

Thus forced to go to the war, Amphiaraus laid his commands on his sons, that, when they were grown up, they should slay their mother and march against Thebes; dispatch by command (the command is carried out in L3-062); perhaps γ²; "forced to go" restates ev 10 and his departure itself is not narrated.
they sent Tydeus to tell Eteocles in advance that he must cede the kingdom to Polynices; the hero dispatched directly; the misfortune behind it lies in other episodes.
Eteocles paid no heed to the message; X, perhaps A (the kingdom withheld).
Tydeus, by way of putting the Thebans to the proof, challenged them to single combat; struggle; perhaps D⁹ (combat that tests), but nothing is gained from it but the victory.
and was victorious in every encounter; victory in combat.

the Thebans set fifty armed men to lie in wait for him as he went away; an attempt to kill the hero on his way back (nearest Pr⁶), no variety number because no chase is narrated; perhaps A¹³ (a murder ordered).
he slew them all but Maeon; the hero saves himself from the attempt on his life (nearest Rs⁹); perhaps I.
and then came to the camp; return.

some say that he was blinded by the gods because he revealed their secrets to men; X, perhaps δ (a transgression, with no interdiction narrated); told only as the reason for ev 2; the census takes this first of the versions.
he was blinded by the gods; bodily injury; perhaps U (punishment); Pherecydes's and Hesiod's versions are not transcribed.
when the Thebans sought counsel of him; X.

he said that they should be victorious if Menoeceus, son of Creon, would offer himself freely as a sacrifice to Ares; the means to overcome the misfortune made known, with a demand that sends Menoeceus to act; the war behind it lies in other episodes; no variety number; perhaps X or M.
On hearing that, Menoeceus, son of Creon, slew himself before the gates; X, perhaps N (the demand fulfilled).
But a battle having taken place; struggle in open battle.
the Cadmeans were chased in a crowd as far as the walls; X, perhaps I (a passing advantage; the battle's outcome is entered at ev 5).
Capaneus, seizing a ladder, was climbing up it to the walls; X.
Zeus smote him with a thunderbolt; X, perhaps A¹⁴ or I− (the blow that turns the battle); Zeus is not a combatant.
When that befell, the Argives turned to flee; the hero loses the battle of ev 1.
as many fell; X, part of the defeat.
Eteocles and Polynices, by the resolution of both armies, fought a single combat for the kingdom; struggle, Polynices fighting for the Argives' side.
and slew each other; X; each both wins and loses, and Propp gives no form for this; perhaps I or I−.

performer: the Argives; the sons of Astacus
undergoer: the sons of Astacus; the Argives
note: In another fierce battle the sons of Astacus did doughty deeds; struggle.
for Ismarus slew Hippomedon; an Argive chief loses his fight; the killing taken as the outcome of a struggle, not as a new villainy.
Leades slew Eteoclus; as ev 9.
and Amphidicus slew Parthenopaeus; as ev 9; Euripides's version is a report of an authority.

Melanippus, the remaining one of the sons of Astacus, wounded Tydeus in the belly; bodily injury, the hero left "half dead"; perhaps J¹ (a wound in the skirmish, p.52), but no recognition follows from it.

Athena brought a medicine which she had begged of Zeus, and by which she intended to make him immortal; X, perhaps D (the approach of a donor) or F (a gift only intended, withheld at ev 9); the begging from Zeus is a flashback.

Amphiaraus hated Tydeus for thwarting him by persuading the Argives to march to Thebes; X; the thwarting, a flashback told as the reason for the hatred, perhaps A, but it harms no one in this episode.
when he perceived the intention of the goddess he cut off the head of Melanippus; X.
and gave it to Tydeus; X, perhaps η (a gift meant to spoil the goddess's intention); no deceit is stated.
who, wounded though he was, had killed him; flashback, told in passing; the one who wounded him killed; no fight described, so no H and no variety number; perhaps U.
And Tydeus split open the head; X; the act completed at ev 8.
and gulped up the brains; the hero's act that loses him the gift (a negative reaction, p.42-43), though Athena sets no test; perhaps θ (the hero unwittingly serves Amphiaraus's aim) or X.
when Athena saw that, in disgust she grudged and withheld the intended benefit; nothing is given; the flight and vanishing of Amphiaraus that follow belong to another episode.
Having succeeded to the kingdom of Thebes, Creon cast out the Argive dead unburied; a harm to the dead, the hero's brother among them; no variety number.
issued a proclamation that none should bury them; interdiction.
and set watchmen; X.
But Antigone, one of the daughters of Oedipus, stole the body of Polynices; the proclamation and the watch defied; perhaps K¹ (the object seized by cleverness).
and secretly buried it; the harm of ev 1 undone for her brother; no variety number; perhaps δ (the burial is the very thing forbidden), with the violation then falling here rather than at ev 4.
having been detected by Creon himself; the villain gets knowledge of his victim; perhaps Ex.

she was interred alive in the grave; a harm to the hero; no variety number (perhaps A¹⁴ or A¹⁵); perhaps U, if she is read as the one punished for violating the interdiction; nothing follows in this episode.

the sons of the fallen, called the Epigoni, purposed to march against Thebes to avenge the death of their fathers; decision on counteraction; the fathers' deaths are named, not narrated, here and get no entry.
when they consulted the oracle; X.
the god predicted victory under the leadership of Alcmaeon; X, perhaps B (the hero designated); the call is entered at ev 7.

So Alcmaeon joined the expedition, though he was loath to lead the army till he had punished his mother; the hero's own agreement to counteraction; his wish to punish his mother is an intention only; perhaps X, as ev 1 already holds C.
for Eriphyle had received the robe from Thersander, son of Polynices; flashback, told in passing; X, perhaps η or θ (a bribe given and accepted).
and had persuaded her sons also to go to the war; flashback; the victims enticed to their danger (it is called his "undoing" at L3-062 ev 6); the first villainy, so still move I.
Having chosen Alcmaeon as their leader; the hero called to lead; no variety number.
they made war on Thebes; the setting out of the expedition; perhaps X or H; the list of the men is a list of names.
They first laid waste the surrounding villages; a harm by the hero's side (pillage); no variety number (perhaps A⁵); a new move by the rule.
when the Thebans advanced against them, led by Laodamas, son of Eteocles; X.
they fought bravely; struggle in open battle.
though Laodamas killed Aegialeus; one of the hero's side loses his fight.
he was himself killed by Alcmaeon; the enemy leader beaten in battle.
after his death the Thebans fled in a body within the walls; the hero loses the battle; perhaps X (the battle's struggle lies in L3-060).
Tiresias told them to send a herald to treat with the Argives, and themselves to take to flight; command that sends the hero away from home; no variety number (perhaps B²); perhaps γ².
they did send a herald to the enemy; X.
mounting their children and women on the wagons, themselves fled from the city; departure in the form of flight.
When they had come by night to the spring called Tilphussa, Tiresias drank of it and expired; X.
After travelling far the Thebans built the city of Hestiaea and took up their abode there; X, perhaps W or T².
the Argives, on learning afterwards the flight of the Thebans, entered the city; X.
and collected the booty; X, perhaps A⁵ (plunder) or K.
and pulled down the walls; X, perhaps U or A.
they sent a portion of the booty to Apollo at Delphi and with it Manto, daughter of Tiresias; X.
for they had vowed that, if they took Thebes, they would dedicate to him the fairest of the spoils; flashback, told in passing; X.
when Alcmaeon learned; the misfortune made known to the hero; the teller is not named; entered before the villainy it reveals because the text narrates the learning first.

that his mother Eriphyle had been bribed to his undoing also; flashback, told as what he learns; a harm to the hero; the first villainy of the episode, so still move I; no variety number (compare L3-060 ev 6, A⁸).
he was more incensed than ever; X, perhaps C.

in accordance with an oracle given to him by Apollo he killed his mother; the one who harmed him punished; the oracle, told as the authority for the deed, gets no entry (perhaps B² or γ²); perhaps δ or A¹⁴, since the Fury follows (ev 9); the "some say" on Amphilochus is not transcribed.
Alcmaeon was visited by the Fury of his mother's murder; harm to the hero; no variety number (perhaps A¹¹ or A¹⁸).
and going mad; X, the content of the harm of ev 9.
he first repaired to Oicles in Arcadia; the victim's wandering after the harm; perhaps X.
and thence to Phegeus at Psophis; X.
having been purified by him; X, perhaps K; not a liquidation by its consequences, since the barrenness of ev 16 falls on him after it.
he married Arsinoe, daughter of Phegeus; marriage (Propp's second form of W), bare W.

I divine that the number of pigs in the womb is not eight, as Calchas says, but nine; X.
So when these things turned out so, Calchas died of a broken heart; the hero loses the contest.
Athena threw a thunderbolt at the ship of Ajax; perhaps U for his impiety (E.5.22-23), which this passage does not name.
when the ship went to pieces he made his way safe to a rock; X, perhaps Rs (no pursuit).
declared that he was saved in spite of the intention of Athena; X, perhaps δ or L.
But Poseidon smote the rock with his trident and split it; answers the boast of ev 3; perhaps a second A.
Ajax fell into the sea and perished; the result of ev 4; X.
his body, being washed up, was buried by Thetis in Myconos; X.
Neoptolemus set out for the country of the Molossians by land with Helenus; "at the advice of Thetis" (the advice of E.6.5, perhaps γ²) has no entry of its own here.
on the way Phoenix died; X.
and Neoptolemus buried him; X.
having vanquished the Molossians in battle
he reigned as king
Helenus founded a city in Molossia and inhabited it; X.
Neoptolemus gave him his mother Deidamia to wife; X, perhaps W² (not the hero's own marriage).
Peleus was expelled from Phthia by the sons of Acastus and died; no counteraction follows.
Neoptolemus succeeded to his father's kingdom; perhaps K of ev 8.

when Orestes went mad, Neoptolemus carried off his wife Hermione; the earlier betrothal ("who had previously been betrothed to him in Troy"), a flashback given as reason, has no entry of its own (perhaps w¹).
and for that reason he was slain by Orestes at Delphi
Philoctetes was driven to Campania in Italy; X, perhaps A; no agent named.
after making war on the Lucanians; X, perhaps H¹ or A¹⁹; no outcome is told.
he settled in Crimissa, near Croton and Thurium; X.
his wanderings over, he founded a sanctuary of Apollo the Wanderer; X.
to whom also he dedicated his bow, as Euphorion says; X.
Demophon with a few ships put in to the land of the Thracian Bisaltians; X, perhaps o (he is not said to be unrecognized).
Phyllis, the king's daughter, falling in love with him; X.
was given him in marriage by her father with the kingdom for her dower
he wished to depart to his own country, and after many entreaties and swearing to return; X, perhaps a (a desire for home) or B³.
he did depart; he leaves the kingdom he married into; perhaps ↓ (he set out "to his own country").
Phyllis accompanied him as far as what are called the Nine Roads; X.

he was not to open it until he should have abandoned all hope of returning to her; the gift of the casket ("she gave him a casket, telling him that it contained a sacrament of Mother Rhea") has no entry of its own (perhaps F¹ or η¹).
Demophon went to Cyprus and dwelt there; X, perhaps δ (of his oath to return).
when the appointed time was past, Phyllis called down curses on Demophon; perhaps A¹¹ (a spell) or U.
and killed herself; X.
Demophon opened the casket, and, being struck with fear; the text does not say whether he had yet given up hope, the condition set at ev 7.
he mounted his horse and galloping wildly met his end; X.
the horse stumbling, he was thrown and fell on his sword; X, perhaps U.
But his people settled in Cyprus; X.
Electra ... smuggled away her brother Orestes and gave him to Strophius, the Phocian, to bring up; X, perhaps B⁶ or Rs; no danger to him is stated in this episode.
he brought him up with Pylades, his own son; X.

whether he should take vengeance on his father's murderers; flashback: the murder (narrated at E.6.23) is told here only as the reason for the question; the question itself ("he repaired to Delphi and asked the god") has no entry of its own, perhaps C.
The god gave him leave
he departed secretly to Mycenae in company with Pylades; the secrecy suggests o.
killed both his mother and Aegisthus; the murderers killed without a fight; perhaps U; by its consequences it is also a new harm, the killing of a mother that the Furies pursue.
being afflicted with madness; no agent named; madness as a spell.
and pursued by the Furies
he repaired to Athens and was tried in the Areopagus; X, perhaps Pr² ("demands the guilty person").
the votes at his trial being equal he was acquitted; the pursuit is not mentioned again; perhaps I (a contest won).
he inquired how he should be rid of his disorder; X, perhaps C.
the god answered that he would be rid of it if he should fetch the wooden image that was in the land of the Taurians; the answer causes his journey; no numbered form matches.
who murder strangers and throw them into the sacred fire; a custom, not an act of the story; X.
when Orestes was come with Pylades to the land of the Taurians; move II breaks off after this entry for move III (ev 14) and resumes at position 9 (ev 17).
he was detected, caught, and carried in bonds before Thoas the king; the detection is perhaps ζ, with no entry of its own.
who sent them both to the priestess; X, perhaps A¹³ (their death is implied, not stated).
being recognized by his sister, who acted as priestess among the Taurians
he fled with her; the flight ends the captivity of ev 14.
carrying off the wooden image; move II resumes here with the object of its quest (ev 11).
It was conveyed to Athens; X.
having come to Mycenae; the marriage of Electra to Pylades ("he united his sister Electra in marriage to Pylades") has no entry of its own (perhaps W, but not the hero's).
was killed by the bite of a snake at Oresteum in Arcadia; X.
Menelaus, with five ships in all under his command, put in at Sunium; X.
being again driven thence by winds to Crete; X, perhaps A; no agent named.
he drifted far away, and wandering up and down Libya, and Phoenicia, and Cyprus, and Egypt; X.
he collected much treasure; X, perhaps a reward (Propp's monetary compensation under W).
after wandering for eight years he came to port at Mycenae; X, perhaps ↓, which is entered at ev 7, where he reaches his own home.
there found Orestes, who had avenged his father's murder; X.
having come to Sparta
he regained his own kingdom
being made immortal by Hera; X, perhaps T or a reward.
he went to the Elysian Fields with Helen; X.
Ulysses, as some say, wandered about Libya; X, perhaps ↑; a summary statement of wandering, the first of the versions Apollodorus lists.

putting to sea from Ilium, he touched at Ismarus, a city of the Cicones; X, perhaps ↓ or ↑: the voyage from Ilium ends in Ithaca (ev 108), but the text does not say he sails for home, and no villainy or lack precedes it.

captured it in war, and pillaged it, sparing Maro alone, who was priest of Apollo; plunder (A⁵), a harmful act by the hero, judged by what follows: the Cicones come in arms against him (ev 4). Move I begins here. The sparing of Maro gets no entry: perhaps E (mercy), since Maro's gift of wine is mentioned at ev 13, but the text does not link the gift to the sparing.
when the Cicones who inhabited the mainland heard of it, they came in arms to withstand him; battle with an enemy army (H¹). Their hearing of the pillage is perhaps B for them; it gets no entry.

having lost six men from each ship he put to sea and fled; the hero loses the fight (I−). Since Ulysses did this move's villainy, the same outcome could be read as I (the doer of the villainy defeated); the rules' I− for the hero losing was applied. The flight gets no entry: perhaps ↑ or Rs, but no pursuit is narrated.
he landed in the country of the Lotus-eaters; arrival, no function.
sent some to learn who inhabited it; X, perhaps γ² (an order whose fulfillment exposes the men to harm) or β (part of the company goes off); not ε, since the one who inquires does no harm.

they tasted of the lotus and remained there; for there grew in the country a sweet fruit called lotus, which caused him who tasted it to forget everything; the men are lost to Ulysses through a fruit that makes them forget. Bare A: nearest A¹¹ (spell) together with A¹⁵ (detention), but no one casts or holds. The tasting is perhaps θ (the victims' own act that lets the harm happen) and gets no separate entry. Move II begins here.

When Ulysses was informed of this, he restrained the rest of his men; the misfortune is made known to him (B⁴). The restraining of the rest gets no entry: perhaps γ (keeping them back, like an interdiction "strengthened or replaced" by confinement), but no violation or consequence follows.

undergoer: the men who tasted the lotus
note: dragged those who had tasted the lotus by force to the ships; the lost men recovered by force (K¹), liquidating move II's A.
having sailed to the land of the Cyclopes, he stood in for the shore; travel and arrival.
having left the rest of the ships in the neighboring island, he stood in for the land of the Cyclopes with a single ship, and landed with twelve companions; no function.

near the sea was a cave which he entered, taking with him the skin of wine that had been given him by Maro; X, perhaps F¹ (flashback: Maro's gift of the wine that later overcomes Polyphemus, ev 18 and 23); the wine is not magical in the text, so F was not written.
having lit a fire and sacrificed some of the kids, they feasted; X; the cave is Polyphemus's, but the text does not call this a harm and nothing follows from it.
the Cyclops came, and when he had driven in his flocks; appearance of Polyphemus, no function.

he put a huge stone to the door; defined by its consequences: the men are shut in and get out only by the ruse of ev 30-31 (imprisons or detains, A¹⁵). The text places this before Polyphemus perceives the men, so it may be his habit rather than aimed at them. Move III begins here; it breaks off at ev 17 and resumes at ev 31.
perceiving the men he ate some of them; murder (A¹⁴). A new act of villainy, so move IV begins, breaking off move III.

But Ulysses gave him of Maro's wine to drink; a means applied to overcome Polyphemus, whose effect is that he falls asleep (ev 23), like the sleeping potion of η²; the wine is not magical, so bare η. Done by the hero to the doer of the villainy.
when he had drunk, he asked for another draught; X, perhaps θ (the victim goes along with the means used on him); the decisive reaction is entered at ev 23.
when he had drunk the second, he inquired his name; the villain asks about his victim (ε); not ε¹, which concerns whereabouts.
Ulysses said that he was called Nobody; the asker gets a direct answer (ζ¹). The answer is false, and its later effect (ev 28) makes it perhaps η (trickery) instead; a single act gets a single entry.

he threatened to devour Nobody last and the others first, and that was the token of friendship which he promised to give him in return; a threat, but one Propp's list includes: threat of cannibalism (A¹⁷; "the last living peasant is threatened with the same fate"). A new villainy, so move V begins, breaking off move IV, which does not resume.
being overcome by wine, he fell asleep; the victim of the means reacts mechanically and falls asleep (θ, Propp's forms 2-3, which share one number).
Ulysses found a club lying there, and with the help of four comrades he sharpened it; X, perhaps F (found, F⁵, or prepared, F³), but the club is not a magical agent.

having heated it in the fire, he blinded him; the cannibal is overcome while asleep. Nearest I⁵ (a dragon "killed while asleep"), but he is blinded, not killed, so bare I. From Polyphemus's side the same act is bodily injury (A⁶; Propp's example is cutting out eyes), and a call for help follows (ev 26); the census hero's side was taken.
when Polyphemus cried to the Cyclopes round about for help; X, perhaps B¹ (call for help); it changes nothing, since those who come go away (ev 28).
they came and asked who was hurting him; X, perhaps C or ε.
they thought he meant that he was being hurt by nobody, and so they retired; X; the effect of the false name of ev 21.
he opened the cave, and standing at the doorway spread out his hands and felt the sheep; X, perhaps ε (feeling for the men); the opening gives the chance of escape.
But Ulysses tied three rams together; X, perhaps η (a ruse against the blind guard); preparation of the escape.

himself getting under the bigger, and hiding under its belly, he passed out with the sheep; the captives get out of the shut cave (a captive is freed, K¹⁰), liquidating move III's A¹⁵. Move III resumes here; the entries that follow stay in move III until the next villainy.
having released his comrades from the sheep; completes the escape entered at ev 31.
he drove the animals to the ships; X, perhaps ↓ (back to the ships) or a seizure of the Cyclops's flocks.

sailing away shouted to the Cyclops that he was Ulysses and that he had escaped out of his hands; delivery by a careless act, like Propp's mother whose loud call betrays her son to a witch; the Cyclops learns the name and attacks (ev 36). The sailing away is perhaps ↓ and gets no entry.
the Cyclops had been forewarned by a soothsayer that he should be blinded by Ulysses; flashback; a prophecy, no function.
when he learned the name, he tore away rocks and hurled them into the sea; attack on the departing hero (pursuit, Pr); his learning of the name is the receipt entered at ev 34.
hardly did the ship evade the rocks; rescue from pursuit (Rs); no form named.
From that time Poseidon was wroth with Ulysses; a state, not an act: X, perhaps A; the wrath acts at ev 100.
he came to the island of Aeolia, of which the king was Aeolus; arrival.
Having entertained Ulysses; X, perhaps D² (greeting), but nothing tests the hero.

he gave him an oxhide bag in which he had bound fast the winds, after showing what winds to use on the voyage and binding fast the bag in the vessel; a magical agent transferred directly (F¹); the showing and the binding belong to the same transfer and get no entries.
by using suitable winds Ulysses had a prosperous voyage; the agent carries him toward Ithaca (return, ↓); perhaps G² instead.

when he was near Ithaca and already saw the smoke rising from the town, he fell asleep; the hero falls asleep by himself, which lets the harm of ev 44 happen (θ). Preparatory for move VI but told before its villainy, so it stays in move III.

his comrades, thinking he carried gold in the bag, loosed it and let the winds go free; the hero loses his magical agent (A², seizure of a magical agent, here by opening it for gold). Perhaps δ without an interdiction, but none is narrated. Move VI begins.
being swept away by the blasts they were driven back again; result of ev 44.
having come to Aeolus, Ulysses begged that he might be granted a fair wind; X, perhaps C (the hero's attempt to undo the loss), made as a request to the former giver.

Aeolus drove him from the island, saying that he could not save him when the gods opposed; nothing is given (F−). The driving out is perhaps A⁹ (expulsion), but only the onward voyage follows; a single act gets a single entry.
he came to the land of the Laestrygones, and [...] his own ship he moored last; arrival; mooring last explains his ship's survival (ev 54) but fulfills no function.
Wishing, therefore, to learn about the inhabitants, Ulysses sent some men to inquire; X, perhaps γ² or β, as at ev 7.
the king's daughter met them and led them to her father; X, perhaps η (luring to the cannibal), but the text gives no deceit.
he snatched up one of them and devoured him; murder (A¹⁴). Move VII begins.
the rest fled, and he pursued them, shouting and calling together the rest of the Laestrygones; pursuit (Pr). The men's flight gets no entry; no rescue follows it.

They came to the sea, and by throwing stones they broke the vessels and ate the men; the pursuers reach and devour (nearest Pr⁵, the pursuer "tries to devour the hero"). Read alone, the act is a fresh villainy (A¹⁴), which would begin a new move; taken as the end of the pursuit begun at ev 52.
Ulysses cut the cable of his ship and put to sea; rescue from pursuit by flight (Rs); no form named.

undergoer: the rest of the ships and crews
note: the rest of the ships perished with their crews; result of ev 53.
With one ship he put in to the Aeaean isle; arrival.
Having divided his comrades, Ulysses himself abode by the ship, in accordance with the lot, but Eurylochus with two and twenty comrades repaired to Circe; X, perhaps β.
At her call they all entered except Eurylochus; the call that draws the men in, judged by what follows (the enchanted drink): persuasion (η¹).
they all entered except Eurylochus; the victims accept (θ¹). Eurylochus's staying out gets no entry; it lets him report (ev 61).
to each she gave a tankard she had filled with cheese and honey and barley meal and wine, and mixed with an enchantment; direct application of magical means (η²).
when they had drunk; mechanical reaction to magical means (θ). Preparatory, but told before the villainy of move VIII, so it stays in move VII.
she touched them with a wand and changed their shapes, and some she made wolves, and some swine, and some asses, and some lions; casting of a spell (A¹¹). Move VIII begins.
Eurylochus saw these things and reported them to Ulysses; misfortune announced (B⁴).
Ulysses went to Circe; the hero sets out against the doer of the villainy (↑).
with moly, which he had received from Hermes; a magical agent transferred (F¹); flashback, written where told.

throwing the moly among her enchantments, he drank and alone was not enchanted; the agent defeats Circe's enchantment: bare I (nearest I², a contest won). Perhaps H with the outcome folded in, or E (withstanding a hostile figure's attempt, D⁸-E⁸).
drawing his sword, he would have killed her; intended, not done: X, perhaps U or I.
she appeased his wrath; X, perhaps U neg. (pardon), though the sparing is not narrated as Ulysses's act.
restored his comrades; the spell is broken (K⁸), liquidating move VIII's A¹¹.
when he had taken an oath of her that he should suffer no harm; X; a guard against further harm, not in Propp's list.
Ulysses shared her bed; X, perhaps W; no wedding is narrated.
Having tarried a year there, he sailed the ocean; no function.
offered sacrifices to the souls; X, perhaps E⁷ (a religious service), but no act of a donor precedes it and the text does not tie a result to it.

by Circe's advice consulted the soothsayer Tiresias; X, perhaps F (knowledge received; at ev 129 he sacrifices "according to the directions of the soothsayer Tiresias"), but what Tiresias said is not told here. Circe's advice gets no entry (perhaps F or G⁴).
beheld the souls both of heroes and of heroines; no function.
He also looked on his mother Anticlia and Elpenor, who had died of a fall in the house of Circe; Elpenor's death is a flashback; no function.
having come to Circe he was sent on his way by her; X, perhaps B (dispatch) or ↑, but no villainy or lack is being answered.
put to sea, and sailed past the isle of the Sirens; no function.

One of them played the lyre, another sang, and another played the flute, and by these means they were fain to persuade passing mariners to linger; persuasion (η¹). Told as their habit; it takes effect on Ulysses at ev 79.
Ulysses wished to hear their song, so by Circe's advice he stopped the ears of his comrades with wax; X, a protective measure; Circe's advice perhaps F.
ordered that he should himself be bound to the mast; X, perhaps γ² (an order), which, kept at ev 80, saves him.
being persuaded by the Sirens to linger, he begged to be released; the victim yields to the persuasion (θ¹).
they bound him the more, and so he sailed past; X, perhaps Rs (his comrades save him), but there is no pursuit.
it was predicted of the Sirens that they should themselves die when a ship should pass them; flashback; a prophecy.
so die they did; X, perhaps I or U (the would-be deceivers perish), but no one acts on them.
And after that he came to two ways; arrival at a fork; no function.
By the advice of Circe he shunned the passage by the Wandering Rocks; X, perhaps G⁴ (the route shown), but there is no object of search.
in sailing past the cliff of Scylla he stood fully armed on the poop; X, perhaps H (readiness to fight), but no fight follows.
Scylla appeared, snatched six of his comrades, and gobbled them up; murder (A¹⁴). Move IX begins; it is never liquidated.
he came to Thrinacia, an island of the Sun, where kine were grazing, and being windbound, he tarried there; X, perhaps A¹⁵ (held by the winds), but no one holds him.

his comrades slaughtered some of the kine and banqueted on them, for lack of food; plunder (A⁵, like the beast that "eats animals from the tsar's menagerie"), judged by what follows: the Sun reports it and Zeus strikes. The stated motive "for lack of food" is perhaps a⁵ (lack of the means of existence); it is a motive, not an act, and gets no entry. Move X begins.
the Sun reported it to Zeus; misfortune announced (B⁴).

when Ulysses put out to sea, Zeus struck him with a thunderbolt; retaliation for the slaughter of ev 88: punishment (U). Read from Ulysses's side, the act is a villainy against him (A), which would begin a new move.
when the ship broke up, Ulysses clung to the mast and drifted to Charybdis; result of ev 90.
when Charybdis sucked down the mast; X, perhaps A (the mast taken) or D⁸ (a hostile creature's attempt on the hero); Charybdis does this "thrice a day", not against him.
he clutched an overhanging wild fig-tree and waited; no function.
when he saw the mast shot up again, he cast himself on it; X, perhaps K if ev 92 were A.
was carried across to the island of Ogygia; X, perhaps G².
There Calypso, daughter of Atlas, received him; no function.
bedding with him; X, perhaps W; no wedding is narrated.
He stayed with her five years; X, perhaps A¹⁵, but the text does not say he was held.
then made a raft and sailed away; X, perhaps ↑, or F³ (a means of travel made), but the raft is not magical.

on the high sea the raft was broken in pieces by the wrath of Poseidon; harm (A); no form named (nearest A⁵, harm in other forms). The wrath is that of ev 38. Move XI begins; it breaks off at ev 110 and resumes at ev 128.
Ulysses was washed up naked on the shore of the Phaeacians; result of ev 100.
Nausicaa, the daughter of king Alcinous, was washing the clothes, and when Ulysses implored her protection; X; a request, here made by the hero himself, so not D.
she brought him to Alcinous; X, perhaps G³ (led), but to no object of search.
who entertained him; no function.

after bestowing gifts on him sent him away with a convoy to his native land; the return home (↓), by a Phaeacian ship. The gifts get no entry: Propp's f¹ (a reward of material value, not a magical agent) is not in the alphabet, and nothing follows from them.
Poseidon was wroth with the Phaeacians, and he turned the ship to stone; X, perhaps A¹¹ (turned to stone) or U; it has no further consequence in the text.
enveloped the city with a mountain; X, as ev 106.

on arriving in his native land Ulysses found his substance wasted; the misfortune made known to the hero by his finding it (B⁴). It announces harms told afterward as flashback (ev 109-113), so by the rule it falls in move XI, before those villainies. His arrival completes the return entered at ev 105.

believing that he was dead, suitors were wooing Penelope; X, perhaps A¹⁶ (threat of forced matrimony): the wooing of a woman believed widowed is told as a state and a reason; its coercive form is entered at ev 111. Flashback.
These, journeying to the palace, consumed the herds of Ulysses at their feasts; plunder (A⁵); flashback. Move XII begins, breaking off move XI.

Penelope was compelled to promise that she would wed when the shroud of Laertes was finished; forced matrimony (A¹⁶); flashback. A new act of villainy, so move XIII begins; move XII does not resume separately, since the killing of the suitors (ev 124) answers both.

she wove it for three years, weaving it by day and undoing it by night. In this way the suitors were deceived by Penelope; deception by other means (η³), done by the victim against the doers of the villainy.
till she was detected; X, perhaps Ex (the deceit exposed) or ζ.

Ulysses, being apprized of the state of things at home, came to his servant Eumaeus in the guise of a beggar; unrecognized arrival (o). "Being apprized" restates, after the flashback, the knowledge entered at ev 108 and is not entered again.
made himself known to Telemachus; recognition after long separation (Q).
arrived in the city; no function.
Melanthius, the goatherd, a servant man, met them, and scorned them; X, perhaps A (an insult; Melanthius is killed at ev 125), but scorn is not among Propp's forms of villainy.
On coming to the palace Ulysses begged food of the suitors; X; the suitors' answer is not told.
finding a beggar called Irus he wrestled with him; X, perhaps H or D⁹ (combat with a hostile figure), but the outcome is not told and nothing follows.
he revealed himself to Eumaeus and Philoetius; recognition (Q).
along with them and Telemachus he laid a plot for the suitors; decision on counteraction (C).

Penelope delivered to the suitors the bow of Ulysses, which he had once received from Iphitus; and she said that she would marry him who bent the bow; a difficult task (M; a test of strength), with marriage as its prize.
When none of them could bend it; X, perhaps N− or Ex (exposure as "the result of an uncompleted task"), but the suitors make no false claim.
Ulysses took it; the task solved (N); the bending is implied by the shooting, not said.

performer: Ulysses, helped by Eumaeus, Philoetius, Telemachus
note: shot down the suitors, with the help of Eumaeus, Philoetius, and Telemachus; the villains punished (U; "The villain is shot"); perhaps I (killed without a fight). Answers the villainies of moves XII and XIII.
He killed also Melanthius; punishment (U); the scorn of ev 117 is the only offense told.
and the handmaids that bedded with the suitors; punishment (U); their bedding with the suitors is told only to identify them and gets no entry.
he made himself known to his wife and his father; recognition (Q).

after sacrificing to Hades, and Persephone, and Tiresias, he journeyed on foot through Epirus, and came to the Thesprotians; X, perhaps ↑ (setting out to undo Poseidon's wrath) or E⁷ (sacrifice). Move XI resumes here.
having offered sacrifice according to the directions of the soothsayer Tiresias, he propitiated Poseidon; the misfortune (Poseidon's wrath, ev 38 and ev 100) liquidated (K); no form named.
Callidice, who was then queen of the Thesprotians, urged him to stay and offered him the kingdom; X, perhaps a promise of marriage (w¹), fulfilled at ev 131.

having married Callidice, he reigned over the Thesprotians; wedding with accession (W), Propp's form 1, "A bride and a kingdom are awarded at once"; the sign for that form cannot be read in the extracted Propp text, so bare W.
the neighboring peoples who attacked him; war (A¹⁹). Told in a relative clause after the victory; placed first as the act that prompts the battle. Move XIV begins.
defeated in battle; battle in the open field (H¹), narrated in the same words as its outcome.
defeated in battle the neighboring peoples; victory in open combat (I¹).
when Callidice died he handed over the kingdom to his son; X; Callidice's death is perhaps β (death as absentation), leading to his leaving.
repaired to Ithaca; return home (↓).
there he found Poliporthes, whom Penelope had borne to him; X, perhaps Q; mostly genealogy.
When Telegonus learned from Circe that he was a son of Ulysses; information that causes a departure (B); no form named, since what is made known is not a misfortune.
he sailed in search of him; departure on a search (↑), by Telegonus. No lack is narrated, so no new move begins.
having come to the island of Ithaca, he drove away some of the cattle; plunder (A⁵). Move XV begins.
when Ulysses defended them; combat (H¹).
Telegonus wounded him with the spear he had in his hands, which was barbed with the spine of a sting-ray; the hero loses the fight (I−).
Ulysses died of the wound; X; result of ev 138, perhaps A¹⁴.
when Telegonus recognized him; recognition (Q). His lament ("he bitterly lamented") gets no entry: perhaps B⁷, but no counteraction follows.
conveyed the corpse and Penelope to Circe; Telegonus's return home (↓), bringing his dead father and Penelope.
there he married Penelope; wedding without a throne, Propp's form 2; bare W, since the sign cannot be read in the extracted text.
Circe sent them both away to the Islands of the Blest; X, perhaps T or ↑.
them Sky bound and cast into Tartarus; imprisonment/detention of family members, opens the move
Earth...persuaded the Titans to attack their father; no clean function for a third party inciting counteraction against the hero; nearest candidate B
gave Cronus an adamantine sickle; direct transference of an instrument enabling the deed
they, all but Ocean, attacked him; open combat
Cronus cut off his father's genitals; the decisive blow of the combat
having dethroned their father; removal from power; no exact Propp subtype for dethronement, nearest is I (or I6, banishment)
them Sky bound and cast into Tartarus; same act, transcribed again under Cronus as hero since the function is the same regardless of which tied figure is tracked
Earth...persuaded the Titans to attack their father; see L1-001/1 ev2 note
gave Cronus an adamantine sickle
they, all but Ocean, attacked him
Cronus cut off his father's genitals
